Sports.title: Robot building and Essien: Yirenkyi’s circuitous path to Premier League
Sports.content:
It is mid-July in Kössen, an Austrian village on the edge of the Alps, close to the German border, at Nordsjælland’s pre-season camp. The Danish Superliga club’s coaching staff, including Michael Essien, are preparing for the new campaign, the stunning scenery par for the course. Every training session is recorded by a drone. The operator with the joystick in his hands? Well, that would be Caleb Yirenkyi, the Ghana midfielder who returned a week early from his post-World Cup break.

He requested to join his teammates in the drills, but after physios told the 20-year-old he required more rest Yirenkyi did the next best thing. It is a story that speaks volumes of his modest character and, a month on, he is poised to make his Premier League debut at Arsenal on Friday after Coventry made him their £26m record signing.

Months earlier, Frank Lampard discussed Yirenkyi with Essien, his former Chelsea teammate, and Coventry beat off competition from top-flight rivals to make him their player after Ghana’s last-32 exit in the United States.

Yirenkyi’s story is another triumph for Right to Dream (RTD), the academy umbrella that, via the Mansour Group, owns Nordsjælland. The club is based in Farum, north of Copenhagen, and developed Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra, Kamaldeen Sulemana and Ibrahim Osman. Mikkel Damsgaard and Patrick Dorgu progressed through Nordsjælland’s youth programme and, in recent years, RTD opened hubs in Egypt and the US. “We are very excited to see a player go directly from the Superliga to the biggest league,” says Alexander Riget, Nordsjælland’s director of football. “Last year there were seven or eight players who were developed in our academy in the Premier League but most of them took a ‘middle step’ before playing – Adingra went on loan to Union Saint-Gilloise, Kudus went to Ajax, Damsgaard played in Italy [for Sampdoria] – but this is different.”

Part of Yirenkyi’s appeal is that he is a versatile performer. After making his first senior start in February 2025, he started every league game for which he was available until departing this month, missing just three matches, all through suspension. He is predominantly a central midfielder but has played at right-back for his country and ended his time at Nordsjælland as a left centre-back.

At the start of last year, he excelled in a 3-1 victory over Manchester United in Altrincham (in front of a crowd of 334) en route to the Premier League International Cup quarter-finals, a tournament for under-21 teams. In Toronto this summer, Yirenkyi’s 95th-minute winner against Panama in Ghana’s Group L opener, a goal set up by his now Coventry teammate Brandon Thomas-Asante, made him only the second Ghanaian man to score on his World Cup debut, after Haminu Draman.

View image in fullscreen Caleb Yirenkyi in action for Nordsjælland. Photograph: Noah Thilemann/FC Nordsjælland

Yirenkyi idolised Essien growing up and Essien’s words of wisdom were priceless. “Sometimes I see some glimpses that remind me of myself when I was little,” Essien said this year. Lampard sees those parallels himself and also shades of N’Golo Kanté’s qualities; Yirenkyi won possession more times than any other player in the Superliga last season (205) and was crowned young player of the year.

Djimi Traoré, the former Liverpool defender, was another major influence. Traoré coached Yirenkyi at RTD in Ghana and quickly flagged his talent. Yirenkyi’s biggest challenge was learning how to harness his power. He initially joined Nordsjælland’s under-19s but regularly picked up yellow cards and was sometimes substituted to avoid the risk of reds. During a first-team camp in the Netherlands two years ago, Yirenkyi was pulled out of a training game because his desire to impose himself caused concerns he could injure key players a week before the new season.

Yirenkyi’s time with RTD was transformative. Born in the town of Bechem, he joined RTD in Kumasi aged nine and arrived in Denmark aged 18 from their academy hub in eastern Ghana, about two hours from Accra, the capital. Riget was Nordsjælland under-13s coach when he first came across Yirenkyi in Ghana. “At that point he was not one where you thought: ‘OK, he’s the next superstar,’ like you did with Kudus. He was a very disciplined student and it was not clear that he would be a professional footballer. At that time, Caleb was also very good at building robots.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Robots? Yirenkyi spent his free time studying robotics, an extracurricular activity while enrolled on RTD’s programme, which provides a pathway into football or further education scholarships. Such was Yirenkyi’s focus, teachers had to remind him to take a break. He won a national prize as a 13-year-old and only the Covid-19 pandemic prevented him from competing in the world championships in the US. After joining Coventry, he was asked what he would do if he were not a footballer? “I’d build robots,” came the reply. Flying the drone this summer, then, was a doddle.

Coventry have signed Yirenkyi for his ability on the pitch but his personality off it is equally endearing. “He is a guy for whom actions speak louder than words,” says Riget of a quiet, low-maintenance and introverted individual. On the morning after Coventry finalised a deal that would increase his salary about twentyfold, Yirenkyi was his usual self with teammates at breakfast. Three days earlier, in his final game for Nordsjælland, he was anything but winding down. “When players make these kinds of moves it can affect them a little, but we had a game against Randers where he was tackling with his head on the ground,” Riget says.

View image in fullscreen Caleb Yirenkyi pictured with one of his robot projects while playing at Right to Dream academy. Photograph: Right to Dream

There are plenty of tales that speak to Yirenkyi’s humility. While in Denmark, he stayed in Farum during the off-season to achieve peak condition, and in 2024 he spent Christmas Eve with the family of the transitions coach, Thomas Kristensen, a former Denmark midfielder. “They had 26 guests at their house and Caleb was number 27,” says Riget. “Thomas’s grandmother is 85 but because of Caleb she watched every FC Nordsjælland game and now she will follow him at Coventry.”

Yirenkyi was always last to leave the dressing room, last off the team bus, only doing so after making sure he and his teammates left no trace; Coventry’s kit staff already appreciate his help gathering loose balls at the end of sessions. “He has been a joy to work with in this short time,” Lampard said. “I think there is going to be a big, big uplift in this boy … we believe he is going to have a really good career.”

When Yirenkyi signed for Nordsjælland, he lived in one of 34 rooms on the club’s campus but, unlike most players who move out after a few months, he stayed until joining Coventry. “He just wanted to stay, use his bicycle and be a professional footballer,” says Riget. “Normally when players leave, we need to help them. But when our operations team went into Caleb’s room, it was empty, absolutely spotless and he had left flowers and a card. He is a special character, for sure.”

Sports.title: Michael Carrick rejects ‘ridiculous’ talk of easy start to Manchester United season
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick has dismissed suggestions that Manchester United’s opening two games against Hull and Ipswich represent a favourable start to the season. United travel to Hull for Saturday’s opening match before hosting Ipswich a week on Sunday. Both sides were promoted from the Championship.

Carrick is adamant neither game will prove easy. “For all of us to know this league, there’s no favourable start, I think it’s a tough start,” he said. “A promoted team away from home is a tough game.

“I’ve been involved in them in the past so I’m fully aware of what’s coming at us on Saturday, what we’ve got to be ready for. So it’s not favourable. It’s an easy thing to throw out there. But it’s pretty ridiculous in a certain way, [we are] not taking it that way at all.”

Carrick guided United to third last season after taking interim charge in January. He became permanent manager four months later on the back of his success in the role. He was asked if leading United to the title this season is a realistic ambition. “It is going to be a jump,” said the 45-year-old. “I would never say we can’t – I don’t believe that. But it’s about what we are capable of doing as a group.

“The run of form we had last season gives us a lot of confidence, but we know there is a whole new step to make. We are pushing to do that. It’s exciting. We have the potential to achieve things and we will definitely give it everything we can. We have to believe we are a good team and can do good things.”

United are hopeful of signing the midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton for less than £75m and remain in the market for a left-back. “We are looking to strengthen the squad, working towards that,” Carrick said. “We are trying to make the most of the opportunities to finish the window stronger than we went into it and are in a good way to doing that so far.”

Mason Mount’s availability for the trip to Hull is in the balance due to a knock.

Sports.title: West Ham condemn ‘offensive and divisive’ chant about Israel winger Manor Solomon
Sports.content:
West Ham have condemned “an offensive and divisive chant” and urged fans not to sing it at their first Championship home game of the season against Charlton on Saturday.

The chant, which relates to their Israel winger Manor Solomon and includes an anti-Palestine message, was sung by a section of the away support during their game against Burnley on Sunday, which ended in a 2-2 draw.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

West Ham said: “We understand that singing and chanting is a traditional and deeply embedded part of the matchday experience. We encourage our supporters to sing loud and proud about their football club and the players wearing the claret and blue shirt, but never in a way that creates division or causes offence among fellow fans.



“We are immensely proud of the fact that West Ham United has always been an inclusive football club, ever since our formation in 1895 … in the 131 years that have followed, that identity has evolved with the club located in one of the most diverse and multicultural areas of London, always open and welcoming to those who become members of the West Ham family and share the values we cherish.



“Equality, equity, diversity and inclusion are at the heart of the club and we believe in the power of football to unite and bring people together. We expect those who represent the club – be that players, staff, officials or supporters – to share those values and ensure that, regardless of individual backgrounds or beliefs, we are as our name says: United. Let’s make sure our support is something to be proud of and the envy of all who face us.”

Solomon scored the Hammers’ second goal on his debut at Turf Moor. The 27-year-old winger moved from Tottenham this month for a reported £5m fee, having also played for Fulham and Leeds in England.



West Ham had a 2-0 lead after Solomon scored in the 72nd minute, but two goals from Zian Flemming, including an injury-time equaliser.

The West Ham manager, Nuno Espírito Santo, told BBC Radio London he was impressed with Solomon’s first outing for the club: “I was happy he scored. It will improve his confidence and he brings very good things [to us]. He is a very talented player.”

Sports.title: Terry Dyson, only Spurs player to score north London derby hat-trick, dies at 91
Sports.content:
Tottenham’s 1961 Double-winner Terry Dyson has died at the age of 91. The Premier League club confirmed Dyson’s death on Thursday and paid tribute to their former winger, who made 209 appearances and scored 55 goals for Spurs in a 10-year spell.

Dyson was part of Bill Nicholson’s 1960-61 side, the first English team in the 20th century to achieve a First Division and FA Cup Double, but one of his finest moments occurred two years later when he scored twice a 5-1 victory over Atlético Madrid to secure the European Cup Winners’ Cup.

View image in fullscreen Terry Dyson shows off the Cup Winners’ Cup at a civic reception in May 1963. Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty Images

“The club is extremely saddened to learn of the passing of our former player Terry Dyson at the age of 91,” Spurs said. “Terry was a key part of our Double-winning side in 1961, scoring in the FA Cup Final. Our deepest condolences are with Terry’s family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

Dyson played for Fulham, Colchester and Guildford after a distinguished spell at Spurs. Yorkshire-born Dyson remains the only Tottenham player to score a hat-trick against Arsenal, which he achieved at the start of the 1961-62 campaign. In 2020, Dyson admitted: “One of them hit my hand. It bounced up, hit my hand and I lashed it in and the Arsenal players went mad.

Quick Guide How do I 

“They ran after the referee, but he never saw it. I didn’t do it deliberately, but it hit my hand and I just lashed it in. To get a hat-trick was brilliant and nobody has done it since. There was a header, a left foot and a right foot. It was perfect.”

Dyson received a small amount of praise from Nicholson, who was well known to be a perfectionist. “He didn’t throw it out willy-nilly, but he said ‘well done’ and I was like: ‘Oh thanks Bill.’ We went out that night and had a few drinks.
