World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.title: Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018922/Chinese Supermarket Chain Recruits Ex-Cons for 2nd Consecutive Year
World.content:
Chinese supermarket chain Pangdonglai has announced the recruitment of former convicts for the second year in a row, expanding its hiring scope to employees who have spent at least five years in prison. The move has sparked renewed debate over the line between reducing employment discrimination against former inmates and upholding public safety.

The plan, announced Aug. 14 by the company’s branch in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, involves recruiting 20 people who have served sentences of at least five years. The store is set to open in October.

Pangdonglai was founded by Yu Donglai in 1995. Based in Henan’s Xuchang City, it has gained a reputation for offering relatively high pay, shorter working hours, and generous time off — emphasizing employee well-being over profit.

Employees work no more than 36 hours per week — in China, the legal limit is 40 hours — and receive 40 days of paid leave annually, including 10 “mental health” days. In the first quarter of 2026, employees’ average monthly salary was 9,600 yuan ($1,400), compared with roughly 5,800 yuan at China’s private wholesale and retail businesses.

Last year, the company recruited former convicts for the first time. Applicants were required to have served no more than 10 years in prison, be under the age of 35, and have a middle school education or higher.

Yu said in a Saturday post on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, that all 30 former convicts hired last year remain employed by the company.

This year, the company looks to recruit former inmates who have served sentences of at least five years.

The move quickly divided opinion online. Supporters praised the company for giving convicts a second chance. Lin Minming, founder of Red Apple Public Welfare, an organization that supports the children of prisoners, told domestic media that the company’s decision to continue hiring ex-convicts, particularly those who “may be facing even more difficult employment challenges,” is “worth paying attention to.”

“In the past, people would make baseless assumptions when talking about this issue — worrying that former inmates would be difficult to manage, unstable, or likely to cause problems,” Lin said. “Now that there’s at least a group of real (ex-convicts) working in a real company, we can see what happens.”

Former inmates in China face significant barriers to finding jobs. Fewer than 40% secure employment because of their criminal records, according to local media.

But others raised concerns. “Many people serving more than five years (in prison) were convicted of serious crimes,” one user wrote online. “Supermarkets are crowded places frequented by ordinary people, including children and the elderly. People who have turned their lives around deserve a second chance, but customer safety should not be overlooked.”

Others argued that giving special opportunities to former inmates is unfair to those who have always obeyed the law.

Responding to the concerns, the company told domestic media that people convicted of sexual or violent offenses are ineligible, and that applicants with nonviolent offenses will be prioritized. It added that those hired will initially be assigned to back-office positions such as warehousing and logistics, rather than customer-facing jobs, and undergo a six-month trial period.

China has been strengthening support for former inmates returning to society. A revised Prison Law, passed in April and set to take effect this November, states that discriminating against former convicts in employment, education, or social security matters is illegal.

Former inmates will also be required to undergo “pre-release education” — including legal and psychological counseling, vocational training, and daily-life skills — encouraging them to pursue employment and entrepreneurship.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Customers crowd a Pangdonglai supermarket in Xuchang, Henan province, May 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018916/Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.title: Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018916/Cold Comfort: What Europe’s Heat Wave Means for Chinese Factories
World.content:
Two gray-green production lines glow beneath harsh white lights, their conveyor belts moving ceaselessly like mechanical rivers. Clanging metal, the rip of packing tape, and the dull thud of cardboard boxes mingle with the hurried footsteps of workers shuttling goods back and forth.



It’s July 10, and the Pinotec electric fan factory in Suzhou, in the eastern Jiangsu province, is running at full capacity to meet several rush orders that have come from Europe in the wake of a record-breaking heat wave.

As temperatures soared in June, exports of Chinese air conditioners to the European Union jumped nearly 73% year on year, according to China’s General Administration of Customs. Sales of fans and evaporative air coolers also surged on global e-commerce platforms.

For the managers and employees at Pinotec, which manufactures fans under the Booster brand, the extreme weather represented a lifeline. After taking a major hit from the China-U.S. trade war and the ongoing Middle East conflict, the sudden spike in orders gave the company an opportunity to expand into European markets and turn its finances around.

But as demand has risen, so have the costs of metals and electrical components, while the market competition has rapidly intensified. Add a weakening euro against the yuan — which erodes the value of European revenue when converted back home — and the factory’s profits remain razor-thin.

Despite the hot market, Pinotec and other small- and medium-sized businesses in China are facing the cold, hard reality that this summer boom could leave them weaker, not stronger.

Final countdown

Every hour, factory manager Zhu Guangshuai anxiously paces through the workshop to gauge his workers’ progress. For the past two weeks, Pinotec has been rushing to complete an order for 500 large fans from a customer in Germany — and shipment is scheduled for 8 p.m. tonight.

Zhu had been confident that just two hours would be enough time for final assembly, but the first hour is already gone and only 223 units are finished. To speed things up, he opens a second, smaller production line, initially assigning two additional workers to help with wiring and soldering, before eventually asking the floor supervisor and materials handler to also step in.

In the end, 15 workers drop what they are doing to help their colleagues reach the finish line — attaching screens, installing handle grips, snapping on base plates, tightening screws. Then, they all proceed to packaging.

Multi-skilled workers who can easily switch between roles have become essential for the factory’s survival in recent times. When the Chinese fan market contracted last year, the company merged two assembly lines and laid off any inexperienced or temporary workers, halving its workforce to just 60.

Away from the factory floor, Pinotec also shut down its 40-person domestic e-commerce operation, dispensed with its content creation team for Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, and dismantled its livestreaming studio.

The company initially made massage guns but switched to manufacturing electric fans in late 2023, focusing on high-powered turbo blowers before introducing a range that includes a palm-sized, handheld model. Profits rose early on, but sales dropped sharply once domestic competitors started to flood the market with cheaper alternatives.

Pinotec’s main markets are North America and Europe, where many people commonly use turbo blowers to clean debris from their cars or backyards. Domestic demand is extremely limited. When trade tensions between China and the United States escalated last year, disrupting global markets, 90% of the factory’s orders came from overseas.

Shortly after the U.S. introduced increased tariffs on Chinese exports in February 2025, an American supermarket chain canceled an order for tens of thousands of units. Then, European customers began asking to delay shipments until the economic outlook became clearer.

The company began losing more than 100,000 yuan ($14,835) a month — and that’s before the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East in February this year. Pinotec lost contact with its customers in Iran for almost six months; finished goods piled up in its warehouse, unable to be shipped or paid for.

Things only began to pick up in late May when Europe was hit by an extreme heat wave, with temperatures soaring as high as 45 degrees Celsius in some parts of Spain.

Inquiries flooded in through Pinotec’s international e-commerce platform: A customer in the United Kingdom ordered 2,500 turbo blowers, along with several handheld models; a Belgian distributor placed five orders over two months, totaling more than 2,000 fans, most bound for France; and other units were also shipped to Switzerland and the Netherlands.

To handle the additional workload, the factory reconfigured its production line. Normally, the assembled fans would undergo two days of charge-and-discharge testing, yet Zhu arranged for assembly and testing to be carried out simultaneously, allowing packaging to begin much earlier.

At 8 p.m. on July 10, the fans bound for Germany are shipped on time.

But Zhu barely has time to catch his breath before a new crisis arises. The electric control boards needed for tomorrow’s production order still haven’t arrived after three weeks of waiting. Pinotec has no option but to absorb the pressure. “We’re already right up against the delivery deadline,” Zhu says. “There’s no room to push it back.”

He decides to adjust the production schedule and bring forward another order. The company can’t afford to leave the assembly line idle for even a day.

And the problems keep coming. Whether it’s the time crunch or reduced staffing, defective products keep appearing on the line and need replacing, while a consignment of plastic casings from an upstream supplier is discovered to have color discrepancies between the upper and lower halves.

All Zhu can do is think on his feet to find solutions.

Changing market

According to Pinotec’s founder, Shen Guangping, the combined effects of rising material costs — prices for copper, iron, zinc, tin, lithium batteries, chips, resistors, and capacitors have all increased in 2026 — and fluctuations in the euro-yuan exchange rate have slashed profits by up to 20%.

Deliveries from component suppliers have also become unpredictable. Suppliers used to stockpile some materials, he says, but now no one is willing to hold inventory; materials are procured only after a customer places an order, affecting lead time.

Sometimes, electronic components suddenly increase in price on the same day an order is placed — but once a quote has been given, the factory often has no choice but to absorb the difference.

Pinotec has taken on nearly 200,000 yuan worth of business without passing on the additional material costs, Shen says. “Our sales volume has grown by more than 50% compared with last year, but there’s almost no profit. We’re mainly producing these orders to win new customers and maintain production volume.”

To drum up new business, Shen has been attending as many overseas trade shows as possible. Last year, he attended nearly 20 across the U.S., Germany, Brazil, and Japan. This year his target is 26, at least two a month.

At recent events, he noticed more customers asking about handheld fans. Sensing an opportunity, he began taking small Booster fans to trade shows and had his technical team develop a mini fan and other new products.

However, the market competition is now fierce. Fan manufacturers in Foshan and Zhongshan, two major manufacturing bases in the southern Guangdong province, have orders through September. Domestic factories are also adapting to international requirements, releasing new product colors and developing low-power, variable-frequency models tailored to European voltage standards and electricity costs.

The EU has imposed strict compliance controls on imported cooling products, and incomplete product certification can expose companies to multiple penalties.

Production cycle

It’s been exactly a week since the Pinotec workers rushed to complete the German order, and now they are halfway through assembling a batch of small handheld fans bound for Japan, which has also experienced extreme heat this year.

Suddenly, the production line is halted. An ultrasonic welding mold that fuses the plastic casing is malfunctioning, leaving scorch marks and gaps in the seams.

Zhu assigns a worker to adjust the mold while coordinating others to assemble the remaining components. Fortunately, the problem has come toward the end of the process — any earlier and the day’s production plan would need to be canceled. Just 24 hours earlier, the factory manager was forced to send workers home early due to a battery shortage.

However, when two representatives from the Japanese client later arrive to inspect the goods, they find the mold still hasn’t been repaired, and delivery is postponed.

As an on-site inspector, Du Kai’s task is to report and handle challenges like these. Before joining Pinotec in early 2024, the 28-year-old worked in sales in Beijing and the neighboring city of Tianjin, and as a property agent in the central Henan province. Rather than relying on commission, he had hoped factory work would provide him and his wife more stability.

After proving his versatility, Du was among those who kept his job when the company swung the axe in 2025. Another group that the company was reluctant to let go was its three qualified solderers, as the role requires delicate skill.

Feng Juan is the factory’s most recent hire. Once a temporary worker employed to apply glue, she was recruited as a solderer after someone else quit. In addition to the salary, the job comes with a 1,000 yuan monthly supplement, yet Feng was hesitant at first — she’d heard that the fumes from soldering were toxic and could affect fertility.

She thought it over, and as she already had two sons and wasn’t planning on having more children, she accepted. Her husband runs a lifting equipment installation business, earning 30,000 yuan a month, but Feng says the family still feels financial pressure. In the past year, the couple has renovated a condominium in their native Henan for their eldest son, and is now planning to buy one for their youngest.

Feng’s eldest son, in his late teens, also works at a factory in Suzhou — a temporary arrangement after he began acting out in school — yet she hopes he won’t end up toiling in a high-stress manual job like her.

Packaging line supervisor Wang Chao is also working to save money for his child. A 38-year-old single father, his parents care for his son back in Henan. He no longer has lofty career aspirations, nor is he interested in job-hopping in search of a better position. His only wish is to put away 5,000 yuan a month and have social insurance coverage.

Even as orders have surged, Wang’s packaging team has dwindled to only 12 workers. He hopes to hire five more, but finding them is proving hard. His two recent hires lasted just six days before quitting because the job was “too tiring.”

Zhu and the factory workers are trying to make the most of this summer boom and, in turn, bring more stability to their lives. They hope that, by evening, their finished fans are loaded onto the trucks and shipped overseas on time. Then, the next day, they can do it all again.

(Due to privacy concerns, Du Kai is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Wei Ronghuan.

A version of this article originally appeared in White Night Workshop. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Workers pack items at the factory in Suzhou, Jiangsu province, July 2026. Lü Meng/White Night Workshop )

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.title: What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018914/What Happens When Chinese Dreamcore Meets the Real World?
World.content:
What if the zombie apocalypse was already here?

In the late 2010s, Chinese indie band Hardcore Raver in Tears imagined just such a world in “Take Her to Wanda Plaza,” a jagged, synth-heavy sendup of the country’s mindless consumer culture. Over pounding beats, singer Lu Yan sang of zombified shoppers and took aim at Wang Sicong, the scion of the Wanda real estate empire and one of the most infamous of China’s “second-generation rich.”

The joke landed because Wanda Plaza is more than a shopping mall; by the 2010s, it had become shorthand for a particular vision of urban life. In the 2000s, local governments across the country saw real estate and urbanization as key engines of economic growth as well as fiscal revenue. Teaming with developers like Wanda, they built vast new tracts of standardized residential districts across the country. These new neighborhoods needed new stores and restaurants, a niche that Wanda also filled by building over 500 Wanda Plaza malls in more than 200 cities nationwide.

At the time, this was all taken for granted as modernization in action. China was urbanizing at a staggering speed, and clean, convenient, and air-conditioned shopping malls like Wanda Plaza were welcomed by both the country’s rising middle class and brands hungry to tap an emerging market.

But for the generation that came of age during this transformation, the convenience and prosperity of the new urban landscape is increasingly tinged with a sense of sameness. Rapid urban expansion did not just change how Chinese cities looked, they argue; it also displaced what anthropologist Xiang Biao calls the “nearby”: the small-scale places and relationships immediately around us through which everyday life acquires meaning.

That longing has since found an outlet online. From obsessively documenting faded Y2K architecture to creating virtual cities and nostalgic video games, young Chinese are attempting to recreate an idealized virtual version of the turn-of-the-millennium city: chaotic but colorful, and full of corner shops, wet markets, arcades, street stalls, and other places to hang out.

The most obvious example of this trend is Chinese dreamcore, which blends aspects of the global dreamcore subculture with elements drawn from China’s own millennial moment. The walking simulator “There Exists Nobody,” for example, invites players to revisit China’s bustling millennium-era towns, where neighborhoods were filled with unpolished mom-and-pop shops rather than sleek shopping malls.

A more sophisticated case is artist Huang Heshan’s digital metropolis “Too Rich City,” which he dubbed a work of “socialist cyberpunk.” Drawing on Huang’s experiences growing up in the southern province of Guangdong, the virtual city mixes modern LED screens with nostalgic elephant slides and swan-shaped boats — both recurring motifs in Chinese dreamcore.

Similarly, Liu Yujia, a photographer better known by his social media handle, “Tiehe West Street,” has built a large following for his dreamcore-style documentation of China’s long-maligned Y2K architecture.

When asked why his work resonates with so many, Huang commented that China’s millennial buildings — many of which have been allowed to fall into disrepair — nevertheless remain vibrant in ways the newer, more uniform apartment blocks aren’t. They’re “a little chaotic, but also more human,” he explained.

Indeed, a key motive of Chinese dreamcore is a desire for more human-scale spaces. Cookie-cutter blocks of shopping malls, chain stores, and gated residential communities have smoothed the rough edges of many Chinese cities, yet their lack of texture — places with which people can establish organic connections — has also led to widespread disorientation and disillusionment.

It is in this context that the “nearby,” the academic term popularized by Xiang, has entered public discourse in recent years. Rather than accepting the numbing comfort offered by places like Wanda Plaza, China’s younger generation is searching for informal spaces and trying to rebuild tight-knit communities.

Standardized urban planning, alongside an increasingly digital economy, has also reshaped people’s sense of time. In 2000, an ordinary Chinese person might experience time through walking to a grocery store, a school, or a park. Nowadays, such embodied experience has been replaced by the “estimated time of arrival” displayed in food delivery and car-hailing apps. This abstraction has rendered interpersonal relationships likewise abstract and fragile, contributing to the desire to return to a slower, less hectic era.

It’s worth noting that Chinese dreamcore is not the only space where the younger generation is seeking shelter and trying to build a digital “nearby.” The anime and fandom subcultures, for example, offer a similar sense of belonging.

Much of this can be traced back to worldwide trends like the loss of “third places” where young people can hang out away from parents and teachers, forcing them into online spaces increasingly divorced from their physical surroundings and leading to what the scholar Keith Hayward calls a culture of “self-infantilization” — such as the global social media craze for kitsch toys like Labubu.

It’s not hard to see why dreamcore-tinged nostalgia would find such fertile ground in both the West and China, even if one romanticizes malls while the other rejects them. These online trends have limits, however. Loosely organized, they lack the capability to make an impact offline. Meanwhile, some of the very offline spaces dreamcore fans like to criticize have effectively incorporated the subculture, positioning themselves as a new kind of “nearby.” Shopping hubs such as Shanghai’s Bailian mall and Beijing’s Wangfujing street now host regular events for anime fans, while Changsha’s Wenheyou has redecorated its commercial complexes to look like vintage markets and evoke feelings of “old Changsha.”

Ultimately, Y2K nostalgia is not immune to the consumerism it seeks to reject. With mounting financial pressure for commercial real estate developers, the Wanda Plaza model may have passed its heyday. Yet the urban landscape it has imposed upon us seems likely to last. They may complain about monotonous “new districts” and their lack of organic street life, but young Chinese continue to find the convenience that modern cities offer irresistible. Chinese dreamcore provides a temporary relief — sooner or later, though, we’re snapped awake by the buzz of our phones.

(Header image: 500px/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018906/China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.title: China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018906/China’s Post-Gaokao Teens Are Spending Big Before College
World.content:
When Wang Yijun walked out of the gaokao examination room on June 8, she immediately started thinking about what she’d do that summer. After three years of putting aside her hobbies and personal interests to study for China’s national college entrance exam, the 18-year-old from the eastern city of Wuxi finally had a summer of her own.

But the summer’s freedom came with a price tag. After the exam, Wang’s parents bought her a laptop costing over 10,000 yuan ($1,400), both as a reward for her years of effort and a tool for her future studies. She also traveled to Beijing and its neighboring city Tianjin, dined out with friends, and enrolled in an audio mixing course.

“I’ve spent around 20,000 yuan in total since the exam,” she told Sixth Tone in August.

Wang’s experience reflects a broader shift taking place across China. This summer — from the end of the exam to early September — students fresh out of the gaokao are splurging on electronics, graduation trips, and new hobbies before they have to buckle down at university.

For many, the spending can reach upwards of 40,000 yuan. For comparison, China’s per capita disposable income last year was 43,377 yuan.

This year, approximately 12.9 million students sat for the gaokao. A report jointly released by XKB Data Research Center and iiMedia Research estimated that incoming first-year students would spend an average of 18,600 yuan this summer, more than double compared with 2020. Spending by family members, such as on accompanying students on trips and celebratory meals, also ranged from 30,000 to 40,000 yuan. Together, the sector — termed the “post-gaokao economy” — is expected to surpass 387 billion yuan this year.

Merchants are moving quickly to seize the opportunity. Electronics sellers have launched promotions that give students special discounts when they present their gaokao admission tickets, while 327 top-rated scenic attractions across the country have rolled out concessions targeting the group. Cosmetic surgery clinics introduced student packages priced below 1,000 yuan, along with interest-free installment plans for customers who show their exam credentials.

But although the trend has provided a much-welcomed boost to the domestic economy, it has also sparked a growing generational debate over where celebration ends and excessive consumption begins. Posts by other young Chinese showing off their purchases, and sometimes sharing tricks to get their parents to buy things for them after the gaokao, soon began to spread online. And parents, facing financial pressure from their 18-year-olds, have now taken their complaints online.

A new coming-of-age ritual

The debate has fueled a popular online meme: “After all, you only finished the gaokao — you didn’t suddenly become rich,” capturing parental concerns over the post-exam consumption fever.

A screenshot of a mother’s chat messages reacting to her daughter’s post-exam shopping list — with items totaling more than 30,000 yuan — has also made the rounds on social media. In it, she says to her child, “How about you be my mom?”

For Chinese students, the summer after the gaokao carries a special significance. Longer than other school-time summers, it is widely considered the last extended break before adulthood brings a new set of pressures — from grad school applications and civil service exams to career choices.

“That makes it feel like a milestone worth celebrating,” Wang said.

On the last day of the gaokao, images of parents waiting outside examination halls with gifts for their children routinely flood domestic short-video platforms.

In one widely circulated video this year, students walked out of an exam room to find their parents holding stacks of laptops, smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, and earphones, jokingly referred to as quanjiatong, or a “bucket meal,” a reference to KFC’s all-in-one spread. Many such gift packages feature high-end brands such as Apple, with a full set costing north of 30,000 yuan.

Wang said her social media feed is now filled with posts by peers sharing graduation trips, unboxing new devices, and making plans to transform themselves during the break.

Seeing others mark the transition with new phones, designer products, and overseas travel, she added, has left many her age who have taken the gaokao but haven’t received or purchased such gifts feeling as though they are falling behind.

Coming from a working-class family, Wang said she tries to balance enjoyment with practicality. For instance, she decided to continue using her old phone because it still worked well.

“Families inevitably differ widely in their financial circumstances, and that’s a reality we cannot avoid,” she said. “If there is something we want, working for it ourselves is a sign of maturity.”

Before the gaokao, Wang added, grades provide a clear standard of achievement. “But once you walk out of that exam room, you’re suddenly surrounded by a world where people are judged by their material possessions. You start to believe that spending, having the latest gadgets, and traveling can fill the ‘void’ that comes with a major shift in identity.”

But, she added, “We’re not just ‘consumers.’ We can create, contribute, and slowly grow as people, which defines us far more than what we own.”

Greater costs

Qiu Jiqing, a professor of women’s studies and family relations at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Lifelong Education College, told Sixth Tone that when she took the gaokao in 1996, her experience was vastly different.

“My parents didn’t buy me any special gifts,” she said. “They simply prepared the necessities I would need for college. When I left for university, I basically took only my bedding and daily essentials with me.”

Qiu said she believes that spending within a family’s means after their child takes the gaokao is justified, especially in an era where electronic devices have become an essential part of education. However, she cautioned that social media and marketing campaigns could overly boost spending and desire for material goods among young people who are still developing their understanding of how and when to save and spend money.

“Learning to distinguish between what we truly need and what we simply want is part of growing up,” she said.

Regardless of whether or not they partake in gaokao celebratory splurging, for many families, the end of the exam marks the beginning of a new stage of spending.

Zhang Chunxing, a mother from the eastern Shandong province whose son took the gaokao this June, has already started calculating the costs of her son’s higher education.

She said that her son’s living costs will amount to around 18,000 yuan a year and tuition will add another 6,000 yuan annually. Transportation, accommodation, and other daily expenses will require additional investment.

“After the gaokao, many children want new phones, trips or other rewards,” she said. “But parents also have to think about the next four years.”

For Zhang, preparing for university is not only about covering costs, but also about teaching her son — who will be leaving home for the first time — how to manage his own expenses.

Qiu, the professor from Jiao Tong University, said that because students spend all their time and energy studying before the gaokao, other skills such as financial literacy, self-management, and independent living are often lacking.

She added that the transition is a challenge for the entire family, as most families are used to a dynamic where parents decide and children follow. After the gaokao, both must learn a new way of relating to each other.

“Students need to learn independence and parents also need to adjust to start seeing their children as individuals who can make their own decisions,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A teenager (right) receives a Nintendo Switch 2 from his older sister outside an exam site after the gaokao in Hefei, Anhui province, June 9, 2026. Han Suyuan/CNS/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018913/After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.title: After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018913/After Nolan Interview Fame, Chinese Scholar Accused of Plagiarism
World.content:
Chinese social media influencer Zhuge Yiyang, also known by her online alias Zhong Shu, has been accused of plagiarizing content across multiple podcast episodes and a Chinese article.

The allegations, which emerged last weekend on domestic social media, come just two weeks after she went viral for an interview with British-American director Christopher Nolan about his recent blockbuster “The Odyssey.”

The 29-year-old from eastern China’s Zhejiang province is currently a Ph.D. candidate in political philosophy at Boston College in the U.S. She also hosts the Chinese podcast “Monologues of a Committed Observer,” which has over 970,000 subscribers on domestic podcast platform Xiaoyuzhou.

Her July 31 interview with Nolan in Beijing was viewed over 18 million times in an X post by video game journalist Geoff Keighley, the son of Nolan’s friend David Keighley.

Subsequent overseas media coverage of the interview — praised for Zhuge’s deeper philosophical questioning — brought her wider recognition on the Chinese internet, where many admired her prolific output, including podcast episodes released roughly every three days alongside her academic, translation, and writing work.

But that acclaim has been overshadowed by recent allegations that Zhuge used translated material from overseas podcasts, books, and magazines without attribution.

Among the allegations, her 310th podcast episode, released in March discussing Iran’s Islamic regime, was accused of plagiarizing an episode of the English-language podcast “Breaking History” released last August.

In the original episode, a guest mentions the establishment of both a health and literacy “corps,” which an AI-generated transcript on Apple Podcasts incorrectly renders as “court.” In her podcast, Zhuge similarly refers to them as “courts” in Chinese.

Social media users also pointed out that, beyond the use of “court,” the surrounding passages also closely overlap with the original podcast in both content and phrasing.

Users also accused Zhuge of plagiarizing a May article in The Atlantic on university students’ use of AI in a similar column she wrote in August for Chinese business news outlet Caixin.

Among the similarities, the first paragraphs of both articles cite the same line from Princeton University’s student newspaper. Zhuge’s second paragraph also describes the university’s honor code as having “lasted through two world wars, the upheaval of the 1960s, the disillusionment of Watergate, and even the rise of search engines” — a line from the third paragraph of the Atlantic article.

In an interview with domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily published on Monday, Zhuge responded to the allegations only by saying, “We live in an age that demands apologies from greatness,” a line she had used in her interview with Nolan. She did not elaborate on how the remark related to the allegations.

In her 364th podcast episode, released the same day, Zhuge said that when she first began podcasting, her life in the U.S. was “a mess” while people in China had been “quite friendly.”

“Now the situation has completely reversed,” she said without elaborating.

Zhuge also said in the episode that she had plans to appear on “a whole bunch of podcasts by Western intellectuals.” She added that American intellectuals also routinely face intense criticism online, citing American political scientist Francis Fukuyama as an example.

The same day, three August book talks Zhuge was scheduled to attend in Shanghai and the central Hubei and Hunan provinces to promote her recent translations of works by German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt were also canceled, with the organizer citing “changes to (Zhuge’s) personal schedule.”

Sixth Tone contacted Zhuge multiple times for comment on the controversy through her publicly listed personal email address, but received no response.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG and Bilibili, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.title: Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018905/Cash Cow: China’s Most Mocked Cartoon Is Suddenly a Viral Hit
World.content:
Poorly animated yellow cows walking on two legs, raw voice acting, and extremely slow pace — these are characteristics of China’s most recent box office hit and viral phenomenon.

Released Aug. 5 after virtually no promotion, the movie, “Niu Lai,” or “Cow Comes,” is named for its titular character: a calf who struggles to stand. The film follows Niu Lai and his herd as they overcome a number of difficulties while migrating, eventually growing up into an able-bodied adult cow unfazed in the face of danger. Except, Niu Lai awakens, realizing that he is still a calf — but he is finally able to support his own weight.

The movie, reported to have no financial backing, earned just 5,500 yuan ($815) at the box office in its first week. But after multiple viewers posted images of the film on social media criticizing it, that number suddenly surged to over 710,000 yuan on Aug. 15, according to ticketing platform Maoyan. As of Tuesday afternoon, it has taken in 20 million yuan, a figure projected to grow to 135 million yuan by the time it leaves screens.

The reason for its explosive popularity? Its absurdist visuals and overall crude production design have turned it into a word-of-mouth viral phenomenon. The characters’ legs rarely move in sync, making them appear like they’re sliding. Close-ups of their heads are overblown and blurry. Transitions between scenes are jarring and illogical, and the characters’ voices are poorly recorded and overly stilted.

The effect has led to highly polarized ratings on domestic review platform Douban, with many giving it either one or five stars. As one highly upvoted comment on Maoyan reads, “You don’t have to watch bad movies, but when a movie is bad enough, you have to.”

Wang Yunfei, the founder of a cartoon studio and an acting animated film judge at various film festivals, told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper, “Professional animators couldn’t produce something this poorly even if they made mistakes. So from a professional standpoint, there’s really nothing to critique. It’s just spectacle-watching.”

The movie’s unexpectedly raw, homemade production has also been regarded by critics and viewers alike as a rebuke to high-investment but poorly reviewed films.

“Niu Lai” was produced by Jingyuan Culture Film and Television Media, based in the northeastern city of Dalian, which was converted from a one-person renovation company, according to corporate data platform Qichacha.

The renovator in question is the film’s creator, 34-year-old Xin Yumeng, who made it alongside his mother, Sun Lifang. The pair reportedly had no background in animation and made the film over five years, without the help of AI. They also provided the voices for the characters, while Sun composed and sang the film’s theme song.

On a domestic radio show, Xin said that he made the film out of a love for animated films, and chose a cow as the protagonist because his father was born in the Year of the Ox.

As for the quality of the film, Xin added that much of the equipment he bought secondhand for the film’s production eventually broke down. “Even the computer motherboards burned out ... The final result has a lot to do with the equipment used.”

Le Fumin, a 35-year-old security worker from Shanghai, told domestic media that he liked that “Niu Lai” was made by two ordinary people, rather than having large film-industry backing. “It shows a bit of rebellion against the assembly-line formula of mainstream filmmaking,” he said. “Why should I only be allowed to watch what the industry feeds me? The kind of happiness I choose for myself is worth the ticket price, too.”

Le said the atmosphere in the theater was particularly relaxed. “Over the course of two hours, the pressure of meeting KPIs at work, the exhaustion of commuting, and all the troubles of everyday life just melted away with the laughter of the whole theater,” he said. “It felt like returning to something simple and genuine — like the carefree feeling of watching random films in a video rental shop as a kid.”

As “Niu Lai” has risen in popularity, fan-made tributes to it have spread online and offline, with some placing Niu Lai into posters for recent international box office hits such as “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey.” Cinema staff have also put up rudimentary, hand-drawn posters advertising the film — and paying homage to its crude animation — outside theaters.

Even stocks of three companies with “niu” in their names — Jinniu Chemical Industry, Goneo Group, and Tongniu Information — shot into the top five trending list on domestic finance data platform Tonghuashun over the weekend, as the film’s title can be interpreted as “the bull market is coming,” domestic media reported.

Other entities are also capitalizing on the film’s virality, creating their own animal-based animated shorts to promote products. On Monday, local authorities for Dongguan City in the southern Guangdong province produced a video titled “E Lai,” or “Goose Comes,” to promote the city’s local specialty — roast goose — garnering more than 26,000 likes on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

For most, however, the movie is simply about having fun. Mak SzeNing, a 27-year-old pet care worker from Hong Kong, watched the film in the eastern city of Hangzhou at a nearly sold-out screening. “I don’t think the movie’s value lies in its production quality,” she told Sixth Tone. “Its value is that it brings a group of strangers into the same theater, and suddenly everyone feels like they’ve found their kindred spirits and laughs together.”

“If a movie can make people laugh, then I think it’s a good movie,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Niu Lai.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018898/China Tests Pausing Countdowns for Delivery Riders at Red Lights
World.title: China Tests Pausing Countdowns for Delivery Riders at Red Lights
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018898/China Tests Pausing Countdowns for Delivery Riders at Red Lights
World.content:
Multiple Chinese cities are implementing a new timer system for delivery riders that factors in the time spent stopped at red lights, easing how long they have to get items to customers.

The system was announced on Aug. 13 by delivery platforms Taobao Flash, JD Food Delivery, and Meituan at a meeting in Beijing with authorities from both Beijing and Shanghai, as well as experts and lawmakers to discuss changes to existing delivery rules.

The same day, Meituan announced the pilot of the system in Beijing, which went into effect in Beijing’s Chaoyang and Tongzhou districts and the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, in the city’s suburb of Yizhuang. Suzhou in the eastern Jiangsu province also began a pilot of the system on both Meituan and Taobao Flash on July 31.

Delivery of food, goods, and special packages in China is a race against the clock, with riders granted little time to complete each order. When a customer places an order via a delivery app, it is transferred to riders, who then choose whether or not to accept it. Platforms require orders to be delivered within a certain time; otherwise, riders incur a penalty.

Before implementing the new system, delivery apps calculated the entire time from order acceptance to a package’s successful delivery, not factoring in the time riders spent stopped at traffic lights. This led to a culture of delivery riders running red lights to make their deliveries on time.

According to a video Meituan released the same day as the announcement, when riders stop at a red light, the app’s delivery page will display a countdown timer for when the light will turn green. A pop-up message from its AI safety assistant then informs them, “Stop at the red light. We’re recording the waiting time. The delivery time for this order will be extended when it ends.”

Once the delivery is completed, the app displays the order number, cumulative time spent at red lights, and a recalculated permissible delivery time based on that figure.

Meituan told Sixth Tone on Monday that it previously estimated time riders spent at red lights based on offline data and algorithmic prediction — a less precise method for e-bikes. With the new system, however, the platform calculates time spent at red lights by accessing real-time traffic light data from traffic management departments, combined with the rider’s location, direction of travel, and delivery route — information provided by the Meituan app.

The new rules will also change how other factors affect delivery time. For example, platforms will extend delivery times if an order is transferred between riders or if adverse weather and difficult road conditions occur. Orders that are delayed at the point of preparation will not influence a rider’s service score.

The estimated time shown to customers will also be adjusted in real time to reduce pressure on riders, using an average speed of no more than 15 kilometers per hour to calculate arrival time.

Li Yipeng, a food-delivery rider in Suzhou, told domestic media, “Now we can clearly see how long we waited at the red light and how much extra time we were given. As riders, we don’t need to worry anymore, and we definitely won’t have to run red lights anymore.”

On Aug. 17, Meituan announced that the system would immediately go into effect in the city of Wuxi in Jiangsu province. The same day, Taobao Flash also told Sixth Tone that the system went into effect today in the eastern city of Qingdao.

Meituan also told domestic media that it is currently reviewing more than 20 other cities as possible extensions of the policy’s scope, and expects it to cover more than 1 million riders by the end of the year.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018904/AI Can Draw Any Building. But Can It Imagine One?
World.title: AI Can Draw Any Building. But Can It Imagine One?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018904/AI Can Draw Any Building. But Can It Imagine One?
World.content:
About six months ago, my friend Steve Barakatt showed me an image of a building he had created with AI. As an architect, I was genuinely shocked.

Barakatt is a Canadian pianist, composer, and music producer — he wrote “Lullaby,” UNICEF’s official anthem. Without any architectural training, he had used AI to design a “piano café”: a building whose roof mirrored the raised lid of a grand piano.

The image was remarkably convincing, and raised an uncomfortable question: If someone who had never drawn a plan or calculated a structure could produce such a compelling design, would there still be any reason to study architecture in the future?

My answer came through an experiment of my own.

In late 2024, “Music on the River” (“Tianmu Qintai”) — a 246,000-square-meter complex on an artificial island in the Tianmu River, in Hengqin’s Guangdong-Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone — was completed. The decadelong project was the 100th building of my career. Over the following year, I looked back on my designs and wrote a book, “The Stories Behind 100 Buildings.” Friends who read the manuscript told me it did not feel like an architecture book; it felt like a movie script.

That gave me an idea: why not turn my life in architecture into a film?

I had explored other art forms before — sculpture, painting, and musical theater — because I believe architects should be willing to cross into broader forms of visual expression. But film presented challenges of a different scale. Recreating decades of urban transformation and showing designs becoming real buildings would traditionally have required enormous sets and a huge budget. So I turned to AI.

I assembled a 10-person team of screenwriters and technical specialists to turn my story into a screenplay and translate it into instructions that AI models could understand. My role was to guide the results and ensure each frame matched my vision. In less than two months, for under 200,000 yuan ($29,650), we completed the two-hour film “The Architect with Three Shades of Blue,” with a score by Steve Barakatt — the composer whose own AI experiments had inspired the project. The experience gave me a firsthand understanding of both the power and limitation of the technology: artificial intelligence is extraordinary at execution, but it does not create.

This brings me back to architecture. AI’s technical power in the field is undeniable, and its advance is inevitable. Architectural design usually moves through several stages: concept design, schematic design, design development, construction documents, and construction administration. The later stages — developing designs in detail and preparing technical drawings — are exactly where AI can be most useful.

No single person can hold every detail of a massive tower in their head. In a traditional workflow, a major project may involve dozens of people coordinating at once, and communication between humans is never perfect. A window is placed here, a beam runs through there, the two collide, and the problem is discovered only at the construction site. It happens constantly. AI does not make these kinds of mistakes. When a task follows clear logic and defined rules, machines are simply more reliable than people.

The profession is already moving in this direction. According to a 2025 report by the Royal Institute of British Architects, the proportion of architecture practices using AI increased from 41% in 2024 to 59% in 2025. Based on my own observations, mainly from China and Canada, adoption is still accelerating; at large firms, it may already exceed 80%.

Yet AI’s power has a boundary, and it sits exactly where architecture begins: concept design. AI can search for solutions only among things that already exist. It can analyze countless buildings, recombine previous ideas, and produce something that appears new. But it cannot generate an idea that has never existed before.

The concept for “Music on the River” came from the name of the district itself: Hengqin (literally “horizontal qin”). I imagined a building shaped like a qin, a traditional Chinese musical instrument, stretching across the surface of the Tianmu River. Steve Barakatt’s piano café, meanwhile, came from his own experiences and passions. That first moment of inspiration — the spark that connects unrelated things in a new way — is something AI does not possess.

This is why I believe architecture will be pushed toward two extremes. The technical and repetitive parts of the profession will increasingly be absorbed by AI. What remains will be two ends of the spectrum: the rare ability to conceive truly original ideas, and the newfound ability for almost anyone to express their ideas visually.

On one side, the barrier to becoming an exceptional architect is rising. The old architect’s greatest advantage was the ability to imagine and draw. With AI, you only need to describe an idea, and the machine can produce the image for you. The technical threshold has fallen, but the intellectual threshold — the ability to imagine what no one else has imagined — has risen higher than ever.

The architects who can truly create may become increasingly rare. The process through which an architect develops — years of demanding study, endless practice, repeated failures and corrections, and the gradual accumulation of intuition and experience — is being shortened by AI.

I have already seen hints of this in the classroom. At Tongji University and McGill’s School of Architecture, where I have taught, I have seen students whose previous work was ordinary suddenly submit projects of remarkable quality. Were they using AI? I cannot know, and I would not presume to accuse them. But I do worry about their development. A brilliant final submission may conceal an architect who has not yet developed the ability to think independently.

That is the paradox: in the future, an excellent architect may need only a powerful idea and the ability to direct AI. But because of AI, fewer people may develop the depth of experience from which those ideas emerge.

At the same time, the barrier to architecture is also falling. You no longer need to know how to draw; with enough experience and aesthetic judgment, you can use AI to generate the building you imagine. In that sense, anyone can become an architect.

Of course, most buildings created by ordinary people with AI will never become physical structures. But even architects cannot build everything they design. While working on “Music on the River,” I designed an underwater theater: as the canopy opened, the building would rise from the water; after the performance ended, it would slowly descend beneath the surface while fish swam past the audience. The idea was abandoned because it was too expensive and technically complex, and it remains one of my greatest regrets.

Recently, however, I asked my son to recreate that theater from my drawings inside a video game. The idea that players can explore a virtual space and encounter something that I could never realize in the physical world gives me genuine satisfaction.

Six months ago, my friend Steve Barakatt’s piano café made me wonder whether AI would make architects unnecessary. Now I see the question differently. AI may change how we design, but architecture will always begin with the human desire to imagine a better place that does not yet exist, and to allow others to see it too.

Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: CoreDesignKEY/iStock/VCG)

World.title: Wesley So keeps Sinquefield crown, bags P5.4 million
World.content:
After crashing out of the world top 10 last year, Filipino-born Wesley So has since gained ground as he becomes the winningest player in Sinquefield Cup history with three solo titles

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-born Wesley So sustained his climb in the world rankings by besting Indian sensation Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa in the Armageddon on Wednesday, August 19 (Thursday, August 20, Philippine time) and keeping the Sinquefield Cup crown in Saint Louis, Missouri, United States.

So, pride of Bacoor, Cavite, and Praggnanandhaa both finished with 5.5 points after the 10-man, round-robin classical matches, then drew the two rapid playoffs, necessitating the decider, where white is given five minutes and black four. So only needed a draw to win the match and the $87,500 (P5.4 million) champion’s purse.

🏆 WESLEY SO WINS THE 2026 SINQUEFIELD CUP!

Congratulations to Wesley So, who defeats Praggnanandhaa in a dramatic playoff to claim the Sinquefield Cup for the second year in a row and for the third time in his career! 🔥👏

After two draws in the rapid playoff games, it all came… pic.twitter.com/MZ0Oc2padA — Grand Chess Tour (@GrandChessTour) August 19, 2026

The 32-year-old So did just that to become the tournament’s winningest with three solo titles, counting his victory in the 2016 edition. Fabiano Caruana also has three, but shared the title with Levon Aronian in 2018.

So, also a three-time United States champion, drew with German No. 1 Vincent Keymer in the first round, before notching back-to-back wins against Dutch star Jorden van Foreest and Caruana.

The first World Fischer Random Chess champion, So drew his remaining games against Praggnanandhaa, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, Anish Giri, and Sam Sevian in succession.

Last week, So placed third in the Saint Louis Rapid & Blitz behind Praggnanandhaa and Javokhir Sindarov.

Congratulations to Wesley So on winning his third Sinquefield Cup title and $87,500! "You can't win all tournaments, not this year!" he told Praggnanandhaa after the game. pic.twitter.com/jeAyOyXB1K — chess24 (@chess24com) August 19, 2026

With his return to form, So rose to world No. 5, behind Magnus Carlsen, Hikaru Nakamura, Caruana, and Sindarov.

On August 23, So will try to complete a remarkable month when he plays in the 2026 Grand Chess Tour Finals with Caruana, Keymer, and Praggnanandhaa.

Rated as high as world No. 2 in 2017, So crashed out of the top 10 last year, but has since gained ground with solid classical play. – Rappler.com

World.title: Northern lights closer? Philippines, Iceland open door to daily flights
World.content:
LUMINOUS. Northern Lights, also called aurora borealis, illuminate the night sky near the town of Thorlakshofn, Iceland, on October 12, 2025.

The agreement could lay the groundwork for daily flights between the Philippines and Iceland, though no airline has announced plans to use the new rights

MANILA, Philippines – Your trip to see the northern lights might soon be easier as the Philippines and Iceland open the door to closer air links, allowing airlines from each country to operate up to seven flights a week between the two nations under their first bilateral air services agreement.

The deal, signed following bilateral air talks in Reykjavik on Thursday, August 18 and Friday, August 19, gives Philippine and Icelandic carriers traffic rights equivalent to one flight per day for passenger and cargo services. These may be operated as direct flights or through intermediate points.

For now, however, no airline has announced plans to use the new rights yet, and there is no confirmed schedule for when services under the agreement could begin.

The new agreement gives airlines greater flexibility to develop routes if they find enough passenger or cargo demand to make them commercially viable. It also creates the possibility of more convenient connections between the Philippines and Iceland even if a nonstop Manila-Reykjavik flight does not immediately go live.

LOOK: The Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights) seen over the sky in Enontekio in Lapland, Finland on Monday, January 25.



Photos by Alexander Kuznetsov/Reuters pic.twitter.com/VLWmd8l2vf — Rappler (@rapplerdotcom) January 26, 2021

There are currently no nonstop flights between Manila and Iceland’s Keflavík International Airport, the main gateway to Reykjavik. Filipinos traveling to Iceland have to take connecting flights, with available itineraries passing through cities such as Paris or North American hubs before continuing to Keflavík.

“This Agreement will serve as the foundation for our future air transportation relationship and will provide our airlines with a framework to explore new opportunities for connectivity between our two countries and, ultimately, between our respective regions,” Transportation Secretary Banoy Lopez said in a press release on Thursday, August 20.

The agreement was signed by Philippine Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Edgar Badajos and Sigríður Eysteinsdóttir, Iceland’s director and chief negotiator for air services agreements. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Claire Castro quote blaming heavy floods on blocked drains is fake
World.content:
The original image contained a disclaimer stating that it was satire, which was removed in numerous reposts of the graphic

Claim: Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Undersecretary Claire Castro said that the recent heavy flooding in the country was caused by drainage systems that were intentionally blocked, in an apparent attempt to pin the blame on the Marcos administration.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted by the Facebook page Nick Vlog on August 17. As of writing, it has amassed more than 6,600 reactions and 1,200 comments.

The post features a quote card of Castro supposedly saying, “Ang nangyaring baha sa iba’t ibang lugar ay sinadya. May naglagay ng takip sa mga kanal para bumaha at isisi sa administration. Ma-konsensiya naman kayo!”

(The floods that occurred across different areas in the country were intentional. Some people placed covers over drainage systems to cause flooding and blame it on the administration. You should feel guilty!)

Another version of the quote, posted across different Facebook groups, cites Castro supposedly saying that she would find the people responsible for intentionally blocking the canals.

Social media users criticized Castro for her alleged statement.

The facts: Castro did not make such an allegation.

The graphic originated from a now-deleted post by a Facebook page describing itself as a satire page. Users who reposted the graphic cropped out the disclaimer located at the bottom of the original post. (READ: SATIRE VS FAKE NEWS: Can you tell the difference?)

There are no official government transcripts or credible reports showing Castro making the alleged statement. On August 18, Castro said that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is continuously monitoring the situation and has ordered a swift response to ensure the safety of people affected by the habagat (southwest monsoon).

In her most recent statement on August 19, Castro assured the public that various government agencies are working to assess conditions and assist residents affected by flooding.

Intensified habagat: The recent downpour and flood experienced in Luzon and some parts of Visayas were caused by the intensified southwest monsoon and the formation of Tropical Depression Neneng.

Though it weakened last weekend, the monsoon once again strengthened during the third week of August. This led to the suspension of on-site classes and a shift to alternative work arrangements for government employees in the National Capital Region and several provinces from August 17 to 20.

As of August 20, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration reported that most areas affected by the habagat this week will see better weather in the coming days.

However, Northern Luzon and Central Luzon, Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Zambales, and Bataan may still experience moderate to heavy rains.

Castro fact-checks: Rappler has previously debunked claims made online involving the Palace Press Officer:

– Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com
