World.title: Azerbaijani journalists visit Shakhi Zinda memorial complex in Samarkand (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 20. On August 20, Azerbaijani journalists visiting Uzbekistan toured the historic Shakhi Zinda memorial complex in Samarkand.

Twenty representatives from Azerbaijan’s leading media outlets are participating in the press tour. Among the participants is Emin Aliyev, editor-in-chief of the Trend International News Agency.

Located near the ruins of the ancient city of Afrasiab, Shakhi Zinda is one of Samarkand’s most iconic historical landmarks. Its mausoleums, built in different periods, blend harmoniously into a remarkable architectural ensemble, densely arranged along a narrow medieval street. The complex comprises eleven mausoleums.

The complex evolved over several centuries, encompassing mausoleums, mosques, and other structures from the 11th to the 19th centuries. The greater part of its surviving architecture dates to the Timurid period.

The architectural details of the complex especially impressed the Azerbaijani journalists. Shakhi Zinda’s architecture reflects the rich interaction of artistic traditions across Central Asia and the East. The octagonal design of some medieval mausoleums is particularly notable, with parallels in Azerbaijani and western Iranian architecture. These similarities highlight the influence of the medieval Azerbaijani architectural school and point to close cultural ties and artistic exchange across the medieval East.

Today, Shakhi Zinda is regarded not only as a prominent monument of Samarkand but also as a vivid testament to the centuries-old cultural exchange among the peoples of the region. For Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan, it symbolizes the historic ties, friendship, and mutual respect between the two brotherly nations.

World.title: Family violence offenders must disclose new relationships under draft laws
World.content:
Serial family violence perpetrators in Tasmania could soon be listed on a public register, face six months in jail if they continue to offend, and need to tell police when they start a new relationship, under draft changes to the Family Violence Act 2004.

The changes are being proposed by the state government.

"The proposed new framework will be one of the most comprehensive in Australia and the world … it's nation-leading," Attorney-General Guy Barnett said.

" It sends a clear message to serial offenders that family violence will not be tolerated, and those who continue to cause harm will be held to account. "

It will be at a judge's discretion whether to add a name to the list and would take into account whether it would identify a victim of family violence.

"Ultimately, that's a decision for the judge," Mr Barnett said.

"But in short, if you have two indictable offences or three summary offences then the judge can make that declaration … and the declaration is in place for a minimum of two years or until the behaviour change programs are completed."

In Tasmania, there are currently more than 400 serial family violence offenders.

"Tasmanian magistrate courts saw a 40-per-cent increase in applications relating to a breach of a family violence order or police family violence order in 2024 to 25," Mr Barnett said.

" This is deeply concerning and demonstrates that there is a cohort of perpetrators who continue to disregard the safety of victim-survivors. "

Guy Barnett says the draft laws send a "clear message to serial offenders". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Other proposed changes include reviewing the threshold for declaring someone a serial family violence perpetrator, and requiring offenders to complete a mandatory behavioural change or rehabilitation program.

Only at the completion of the program can a serial family violence perpetrator declaration be lifted.

If no effort is made to engage in a behaviour change program, then the declaration will remain for a minimum of two years.

Bree Klerck from the Tasmanian Family and Sexual Violence Alliance said the behaviour change programs were vital.

Bree Klerck says serial domestic violence offenders are falling through the gaps. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"Serial offenders are a real problem. We're hearing that quite a lot from police as well and that's putting a lot of pressure on the system," she said.

"If we're not seeing those behaviour changes, then the opportunity to continue offending in other relationships is going to happen.

"At the moment, we're seeing a lot of offenders falling through the gaps, and women and children are still feeling unsafe. That is really important to make sure those measures are in place."

Concerns about high number of police family violence orders issued towards women On-the-spot family violence orders are designed to protect those impacted by domestic and family violence. But advocates say they can unfavourably backfire on victim-survivors.

A person's previous family violence convictions in another state or territory can be considered when determining whether someone is a serial family violence perpetrator under the changes.

Courts could also be given additional powers to impose conditions to prevent further family violence and protect current, former or potential partners.

Minister for Women and the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence Jo Palmer said, "we cannot see the continuation of the destruction that family violence is having on our communities".

" There must be consequences for this sort of behaviour. "

Jo Palmer says the actions of perpetrators impacts on the community. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

'Very long waitlist' for rehabilitation program

In Tasmania, a magistrate can make attending a rehabilitation program part of a family violence order.

The family violence offender intervention program has a waitlist of more than 200 people. It runs every 10 weeks and takes 12 participants each time.

In March, the wait time for the program was 18 to 24 months in the state's south, and six to nine months in the north and north-west.

Engender Equality chief executive Alina Thomas said the state also had a "very long waitlist" for support services.

Alina Thomas says there needs to be an equal investment in support services for victim-survivors. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

"We have about 200 people on our waitlist, so we need to make sure that while we're improving the criminal justice response, we're also making sure there's an equal investment in building up the resources for victim-survivors," she said.

" I would like to see alongside these reforms that we have a focus on victim survivor support services, especially access to non-government services. "

Ms Thomas also questioned whether having perpetrators listed on a public registry would impact the safety and privacy of victim-survivors.

Early intervention, more funding needed

Women's Legal Service Tasmania principal solicitor Zoe Craven said the reforms were only the tip of the iceberg of required changes.

"There needs to be a much longer process of consultation, especially with victim-survivor groups and the services that support and advocate for them," Ms Craven said.

"That [should] be followed by more extensive reforms that invest in early intervention, prevention and broader-scale system reform.

"More investment more broadly in education, health, housing: That's what is going to keep victim-survivors and their children safe.

Ms Craven said early intervention and systemic change were needed.

"You're not going to impact the levels of family violence that we're seeing simply by locking up offenders for longer or putting them on a register or making them report their new relationships," she said.

"We need to see that broader systems change and early intervention before victim-survivors and their children are safer."

The Tasmanian government said the draft legislation will be released by the end of the year for public consultation.

World.title: Security issues loom large over Prince Harry and Meghan's return to UK
World.content:
Prince Harry and his family's access to taxpayer-funded security is again in the spotlight after their plans to move back to the United Kingdom were revealed this week.

The issue has been a source of tension between the Duke of Sussex, Buckingham Palace and British authorities for several years.

Prince Harry, his wife Meghan and their two children are expected to relocate to England from the United States, where they have lived since 2020, before the end of this month.

It remains unclear whether a stalemate over their safety has been resolved.

On Thursday, local time, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Sussexes' security arrangements were a "private matter".

"It's a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the move that they are making," he said.

Prince Harry has previously styled the issue as a deal-breaker, and the family's decision to return to England came as a surprise.

Last year the duke told the BBC he "can't see a world" in which he would bring his family to the UK, due to safety concerns.

What's behind Harry and Meghan's UK return While a move to London now brings Meghan and Harry in closer proximity to the royal family, it does not solve the Windsor's complicated dynamics or the deep rift between two brothers.

The Sussexes were stripped of their publicly funded protection around the time they ceased to be working royals in early 2020.

Since then, their eligibility for it during rare visits to the UK were assessed on a case-by-case basis by an independent committee comprising public servants, police and members of the royal household.

The duke launched an unsuccessful legal challenge over their decision to revoke his family's protection.

His request for royal protection during a visit to the UK last month was rejected.

Prince Harry and Meghan have been paying a private security team in California and it is not clear whether they will join the royals when they relocate to Britain.

"I think what we can anticipate is that a threshold of security must have been reached that is satisfactory for Harry and Meghan and the children," royal commentator Afua Hagan told the ABC.

"If that hadn't been reached this would not be happening. We don't know what the security arrangements are, we don't know where they're going to live, apart from we know there'll be a private residence outside of London."

Local media has reported the royal couple have enrolled their children Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, in UK schools.

Relationship with royal family remains strained

It is not clear why they have decided to return to England, although it has been suggested it could be to spend more time with King Charles III who was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

Prince Harry's relationship with his family has been strained for several years.

He and his wife gave an interview to Oprah Winfrey in 2021 in which they criticised the royal family and spoke about racism in the institution.

The duke's 2023 autobiography, which included claims of a physical altercation with his brother in 2019, is also believed to have burned several bridges.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has not travelled to the UK with her husband since Queen Elizabeth II's funeral in 2022. It's understood that the duke and his brother, Prince William, have not spoken since then.

Last year, Prince Harry and the king had a brief meeting at Clarence House which lasted less than an hour. There are conflicting accounts of how that went.

King Charles III is understood to be happy about the prospect of spending more time with his son's family. (Reuters: Carl Court)

It is understood King Charles III was made aware of the Sussexes' plans on Sunday, local time, and that he welcomed the opportunity to spend more time with them.

The ABC understands there are no plans for Prince Harry and Meghan to return to their roles as working royals.

Adding another complexion to the duke and his family's move is his strained relationship with the British press which he accuses of racism and privacy breaches.

He and his wife have launched multiple legal cases against newspaper publishers in the country.

They have also kept their children's lives and faces largely away from cameras in Los Angeles, something that appears unlikely to happen when they return to the UK.

World.title: Five key takeaways from triple murderer Erin Patterson's appeal
World.content:
Triple murderer Erin Patterson made a bid this week in the Court of Appeal to have her convictions overturned. It could take weeks or months for the judges to make a ruling.

Patterson was convicted last year of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder after a deadly beef Wellington lunch laced with death cap mushrooms she served her relatives in 2023.

A Victorian Supreme Court jury found her guilty of murdering in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, along with Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson. Mrs Wilkinson's husband, Ian Wilkinson, was gravely ill following the lunch, but survived.

Don Patterson (left), Heather Wilkinson (centre) and Gail Patterson (right) all died after consuming a beef Wellington meal laced with death cap mushrooms. (ABC News)

Patterson was handed three life sentences with a non-parole period of 33 years, meaning she could be let out of jail in the year 2056 at the age of 82.

Her lawyers argued this week her convictions should be overturned because of problems during her trial that amount to a miscarriage of justice.

The Leongatha mother has always pleaded innocence and claimed she did not know the mushrooms in the beef Wellington were poisonous.

Here are some key takeaways from what happened this week:

1. Jury accommodation

The jury in the murder trial was placed in the same hotel in Morwell as the police informant and some solicitors from the Office of Public Prosecutions for several days during deliberations over the verdicts.

The defence argued this was a "catastrophic" error as it could have led to direct or indirect contact between a jury member and a party to the trial.

A court sketch of Erin Patterson during her appeal hearing on Wednesday. (Supplied: Anita Lester)

Patterson's barrister, Richard Edney, said the defence team had no idea exactly what happened in the hotel during the days of accommodation overlap and that prosecutors should have submitted material about it.

The Office of Public Prosecutions (OPP) dismissed the defence's argument as "far-fetched" and without substance.

OPP lawyer Brendan Kissane KC said a letter from the judge's associate and a letter from the prosecution at the time indicated there was no contact between the jury and any parties staying at the same hotel.

2. The SD card of photos

One of the key grounds that Patterson's lawyers argued should lead to her murder conviction being overturned centres on an SD card found in her home during a police search.

An examination of the SD card by authorities found several photos, dated to April and May 2020, showing various photos of mushrooms and shots of Patterson's children.

Photos of mushrooms found on the SD card. (Supreme Court of Victoria)

The question both prosecutors and Patterson's lawyers argued was: Should these photos have been included as trial evidence?

Justice Christopher Beale, who oversaw the murder trial last year, changed his mind on the issue by initially ruling the photos out, before bringing them in as evidence a few days later.

Listen to The Case of podcast | Mushroom Lunch Mushroom Lunch continues to follow all proceedings related to Erin Patterson's triple murder conviction in July 2025.

3. Life in jail

The court heard this week that Patterson has remained in protective custody, as she was at the time of her sentencing.

Mr Kissane said Patterson had access to a library, recreation centre, exercise yard and treadmill in prison. She also has regular video calls with her children and engages in hobbies such as crocheting.

As Mr Kissane listed these things, ABC reporters in the courtroom said Patterson could be seen on the video link from Dame Phyllis Frost women's prison closing her eyes and shaking her head.

Mr Kissane also said Patterson had access to a chaplain and counselling services.

Erin Patterson is imprisoned at Dame Phyllis Frost Centre in Melbourne's west. (ABC News: Barrie Pullen)

Patterson's lawyers raised concerns about her being kept in solitary confinement, which the prosecution disputed.

Defence barrister Mr Edney said his client's custody arrangement was in line with the United Nations definition of solitary confinement of 22 hours a day alone without contact.

4. Prosecution's appeal for a harsher sentence

Yesterday, the prosecution lodged an appeal for Patterson to serve life in jail with no parole.

Mr Kissane argued even if she was entitled to the possibility of parole, the current 33 years was not enough.

He said the sentencing judge found the three murders and one attempted murder involved cruelty, betrayal and significant planning.

He also said Patterson had time to intervene after her victims had eaten the deadly meal and showed no pity.

Patterson's legal team including barristers Richard Edney and Veronika Drago arriving at court on Thursday. (ABC News)

5. Ian Wilkinson attended

The sole survivor of the deadly lunch, Ian Wilkinson, travelled from his Gippsland home to Melbourne this week to watch the appeal hearings.

He sat in the front row of the public gallery and was supported by family.

Ian Wilkinson and family attended the appeal hearings this week in Melbourne. (ABC News)

The Baptist pastor also attended each day of the 11-week trial in Morwell last year.

He spent nearly two months at the Austin Hospital in Melbourne back in 2023 following the beef Wellington that Patterson served him.

Patterson's estranged husband Simon did not attend the hearings this week.

World.title: 'Making trouble': Court unseals Murdoch family succession documents
World.content:
It was in 2024 at an unremarkable courthouse in Reno where members of the Murdoch family gathered to battle it out.

Rupert Murdoch was trying to change his family trust to consolidate control of his media empire into the hands of his eldest son, Lachlan Murdoch, rather than split it equally among his children.

After months of consideration, the court denied his bid.

The Nevada court never publicly released its detailed findings or explained why the commissioner ruled against Rupert and Lachlan — until now.

In a 96-page document unsealed overnight, Commissioner Edmund Gorman detailed how the plan to change the trust was a "carefully crafted charade", concluding that Rupert and Lachlan acted in "bad faith" towards Lachlan's siblings — James, Elisabeth and Prudence.

Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch attempted to remove control of the media empire from Prudence MacLeod nee Murdoch, James Murdoch and Elisabeth Murdoch. (AP/Reuters)

The document had not been previously released, but The New York Times and other outlets had cited the findings in their reporting.

It reveals how the succession battle unfolded in court, as well as the key role Australian media executive and Australia Post chair Siobhan McKenna — previously Lachlan's closest advisor — played in the plans to alter the trust.

In 2025, the family reached a deal that guaranteed Lachlan would retain control of his father's media empire after the elderly patriarch's death, with the other three eldest siblings to each receive more than $US1 billion ($1.52 billion) for their shares in the companies.

But the scars from the deep rift in the family are laid bare in the judgement — a culmination of decades of public bickering and a bitter battle in court.

Rupert Murdoch and then-wife Anna Murdoch with Lachlan, James and Elisabeth at their New York home in the 1980s. (Peter Carrette Archive/Getty Images)

The 'irrevocable' trust at centre of court battle

The original Murdoch trust dates back to 1970, according to the court document, when Rupert elected to create a trust "in an effort to avoid high Australian death taxes".

The succession plan, or lack thereof, was cemented in 1999, after Rupert divorced his second wife Anna Torv.

Then was born the Murdoch Family Trust — an "irrevocable" agreement that stipulated control of the business be equally split between Rupert and his then offspring.

Here's the Murdoch family tree to bring you up to date With Rupert having been married four times and having six children, here is a look at who's who in the Murdoch family tree.

It would mean that after Rupert's death, control of Fox Corporation and News Corporation would have been evenly divided between Rupert's four oldest children.

It included a clause that allowed Rupert to amend the children's sub-trusts if it was "in the best interests of such beneficiaries", which formed the basis of Rupert and Lachlan's arguments in court.

Rupert and Lachlan hatched a plan, dubbed Project Family Harmony, which Commissioner Gorman described as "perhaps too optimistic".

The plan would ensure that Lachlan would retain control of the company.

Siobhan McKenna was Lachlan Murdoch's trusted lieutenant. (Supplied: Menzies Foundation)

But the new court findings detail how News Corp powerbroker Siobhan McKenna was central to Project Family Harmony, as a trusted lieutenant to Lachlan.

Commissioner Gorman wrote that the project "had its origins with Siobhan McKenna and Lachlan Murdoch in the middle of 2023", with Rupert only brought into the plan later that year.

At the time, Ms McKenna was in her first year of working as chair of Australia Post, after being appointed by the Albanese government in late 2022.

"The evidence shows that it was Lachlan Murdoch's MD, Siobhan McKenna … that was the driving force behind Project Family Harmony until the special meeting [in December 2023]," he wrote.

"It was Siobhan McKenna who organised the meetings, prepared each meeting agenda, and interfaced with the attorneys … and prepared talking points [for Rupert] to use with all four of his daughters."

According to the judgement, she also vetted candidates for key roles, using Fox security staff to help do the background check.

Among the disqualifying factors was "any association with or like for any other Murdoch person".

Ms McKenna also went with Rupert to meet with his ex-wife Wendi Deng, subsequently sending her a draft settlement agreement to allow amendments for the sub-trusts of Chloe and Grace Murdoch, the document said.

Ms McKenna cut ties with Lachlan and the global media empire last year.

Rupert Murdoch wanted to hand the reins of his media empire to Lachlan rather than James. (Supplied: News Corp)

A 'carefully crafted charade'

In seeking the court's approval to rewrite the family trust, Rupert had to show he was acting in "good faith" with the sole purpose of benefiting all his heirs.

But the court's probate commissioner ruled that Rupert and Lachlan had brought the case in "bad faith".

Commissioner Gorman described the plan as a "carefully crafted charade" designed to protect Lachlan's power, "regardless of the impacts such control would have over the companies of the beneficiaries".

He wrote that Rupert and Lachlan's managing directors were "motivated primarily by the desire to serve Rupert [and Lachlan] Murdoch's wishes by eliminating the 'math problem' that the objecting children's [managing directors] could outvote Lachlan Murdoch after Rupert Murdoch's death and alter the companies' editorial stance."

An episode of Succession reportedly sparked secret discussions among Rupert Murdoch's children about his death. (Supplied: HBO/Macall B Polay)

The proceedings revealed that the TV death of Succession protagonist Logan Roy in April 2023 sparked discussion among some of the Murdoch children about a PR strategy for their father's death.

"Setting off these discussions was the episode of the HBO drama Succession," the commissioner wrote, "where the patriarch of the family dies, leaving his family and business in chaos."

And although Mr Gorman confirmed the children met and discussed "arrangements (or the lack of arrangements) for Rupert Murdoch's funeral and certain management issues at Fox and News", there was "grossly insufficient" evidence to show that Elisabeth or Prudence were part of any plan or scheme to join forces with James after Rupert's death.

The decision also shows that James, Elisabeth and Prudence had "disavowed any plan to oust their brother", and they did not share "any singleness of purpose in changing the management of Fox News".

"The effort was an attempt to stack the deck in Lachlan Murdoch's favour after Rupert Murdoch's passing so that the succession would be immutable," the commissioner wrote.

The court ruled that Rupert and Lachlan Murdoch had brought the case in "bad faith". (GC Images: Adrian Edwards)

How Rupert Murdoch became deeply suspicious of his son James

Despite once being groomed as a succession frontrunner, and his rapid ascension in the family business, James left the empire in 2020.

He resigned from News Corporation's board after criticising its newspapers' "ongoing denial of the role of climate change" in bushfires across Australia that year.

Although James, Elisabeth and Prudence are all understood to be less conservative than Lachlan, James had been particularly critical of the organisation's media outlets in the past, having also taken issue with Fox News's coverage of conspiracy theories about voting machines in the 2020 US election, which Mr Trump lost to Joe Biden.

Executives in the company suspected James of briefing journalists on the family, the court document said. (Reuters: Fred Greaves)

The court ruling details how meetings for Project Family Harmony ran risk-scenarios for Rupert's legacy, including one that discussed what would happen if "post-[Rupert Murdoch], troublesome beneficiary achieves control".

Commissioner Gorman found: "The evidence is unequivocal and uncontested that Project Family Harmony references to a 'difficult' or 'troublesome' beneficiary are references to James Murdoch."

James's ever-souring relationship with his elder brother and father has been well-reported, but Commissioner Gorman points to Rupert's suspicion of his son as a key reason why Project Family Harmony got the green light.

"Rupert Murdoch was brought into the plan … under the false assumption that James Murdoch was 'making trouble' by fuelling press speculation about governance of the [Murdoch Family Trust] after Rupert Murdoch's passing," he wrote.

The family later reached a deal that guarantees Lachlan (right) will retain control of the empire. (Reuters: Mike Blake)

But Commissioner Gorman said Rupert's beliefs about James's dealings with the press were "unsubstantiated".

In one example, the commissioner said Lachlan and others within the company believed James, or someone acting on his behalf, had leaked information to Financial Times journalist Alex Barker about the details of the family trust.

But Commissioner Gorman wrote, "at trial, Lachlan Murdoch admitted that he did not have any proof that James Murdoch or his associates had briefed Alex Barker".

A similar suspicion arose regarding a book published around that time called The Successor, an unauthorised biography of Lachlan written by Australian journalist Paddy Manning, who is now an investigative reporter at the ABC.

Lachlan Murdoch pictured in 2022. (Supplied: Lionel Hanh Picture Group for Fox Sports)

But the evidence in Reno pointed elsewhere. Commissioner Gorman found that for Manning's book it was Lachlan's own adviser, Ms McKenna, who had been a significant source, giving more than 14 hours of interviews plus follow-up correspondence.

"The evidence demonstrates that Lachlan Murdoch falsely told his father, without proof, that James Murdoch or his associates were sources for The Successor," the commissioner wrote.

"He did not tell his father that Siobhan McKenna had been involved, with his authorisation."

Commissioner Gorman also described Rupert's concern that his younger son would vehemently oppose Project Family Harmony.

"They assumed James Murdoch would be 'very hostile to this and would basically pull out the stops to block it,'" he wrote.

Murdoch family granted private trial

The bitter family feud lasting decades has captivated the world and triggered international headlines — with a global media empire at stake.

The court ruling confirmed the family had sought counselling back in 2010, with all present except Prudence, in order to "unpack some of the tensions or problems in the family".

The process was described by Elisabeth as "painful", while Lachlan said the siblings aired "petty grievances" against Rupert before "they all ended up hating each other".

The 2024 court case brought one family chapter to a close.

While the court denied Rupert's bid to change the family trust, the family later reached a deal that guarantees Lachlan will retain control of his father's media empire after the elderly patriarch's death.

We now know what happens to Rupert Murdoch's empire when he dies The deal secures Rupert Murdoch's legacy as the founder of the world's most powerful conservative media empire.

The trial held in September 2024 was a closed-door hearing, despite a petition from the non-profit organisation Our Nevada Judges to televise the trial.

Six news organisations — the Associated Press, CNN, National Public Radio, The New York Times, Reuters, and The Washington Post — also filed a petition to unseal court proceedings and documents.

The petitions were rejected before the trial began, with the judge ruling that the case is "essentially a private legal arrangement".

The 96-page document of the commissioner's findings was unsealed yesterday after Our Nevada Judges won an appeal this week.

World.title: Outlook worsens for government to meet 1.2 million houses promise
World.content:
Federal government advisors have extended their outlook on when 1.2 million homes will be built, as developers, builders and investors wait to see whether the housing market will settle or fall further in the wake of interest rate rises and an overhaul of the tax system.

The National Housing Supply and Affordability Council originally forecast the National Housing Accord would deliver 1.2 million new homes by June 2029, then in April revised this to September 2030, but now expects the target will not be reached until the end of 2030.

The May federal budget contained a major rewrite of tax perks for housing investors, ending negative gearing benefits on existing properties bought after budget night and tightening the discount from capital gains tax when investment properties are sold.

Since then, the Reserve Bank also lifted the official cash rate for a third time this year to 4.35 per cent, and the ongoing conflict in Iran has continued to put pressure on fuel and construction costs.

The housing minister has said interest rates are the overwhelming driver of the recent downturn in the housing market.

NSW, Tasmania lag on housing targets

While the council revised down its outlook for the 1.2 million-home target, it also found approvals were up by 26 per cent since the National Housing Accord began, and commencements had risen by 15 per cent.

Victoria has built about 32 per cent of its share of the target, WA about 29 per cent of its obligations, South Australia 28 per cent, Queensland 24 per cent, and NSW 21 per cent.

While Victoria is expected to meet its share of the Housing Accord just behind deadline in December 2029, the council has revised down its outlook for NSW, saying the nation's most populous state will not meet its obligations until March 2032.

The ACT has built 34 per cent of its share, the NT 28 per cent and Tasmania has built 16 per cent of its share, with the Apple Isle's Accord share not expected to be met until June 2034.

The federal government says across every state and territory, approvals are up from the year before, and planning reforms increasing density, unlocking land and investing in infrastructure are strengthening the housing pipeline.

And it argues that has been despite impacts on construction from the war in Iran, particularly on fuel prices.

In an update overnight, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil and Environment Minister Murray Watt said housing construction prices were stabilising from a yearly increase of 17 per cent in 2022, down to 3.8 per cent, in line with inflation.

There have been 308,000 homes completed since the Accord began, with 80,000 homes green-lit for construction since the Albanese government came to power and homes being built faster — in part due to an overhaul of environment laws passed last year.

"Our focus is simple — keep building, keep removing roadblocks and get more Australians into homes," Ms O'Neil said in a statement.

Clare O'Neil says the federal government is turning around a housing system "that wasn't working for Australians". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

But the opposition has highlighted that at the current pace, the government was expected to fall about 200,000 homes short of what it agreed in the National Housing Accord.

Master Builders chief executive Denita Wawn said economic uncertainty was making it "harder to convert demand into actual construction activity".

"Demand for homes hasn't disappeared; the problem is that too many projects no longer stack up financially," Ms Wawn said.

"Builders and tradies need certainty that projects they take on will remain commercially viable, and the federal government must work to restore positive market conditions that support investment, a task made harder by the recent federal budget.

"Our latest forecasts show Australia is tracking to fall 204,000 homes short of the National Housing Accord target. We expect our next projections, which will take into account the impacts of the Middle East conflict and the federal budget, to show that shortfall growing even further."

CBA home loan applications down 15pc Australia's largest home lender, the Commonwealth Bank, has seen home loan applications tumble 15 per cent since May.

The sector fears the recent housing downturn could hurt supply further if it becomes protracted.

The government has held fast to its budget forecast that house price growth will only slow by 2 per cent over the medium-term, despite the deepening downturn since May that has brought falling property prices and a sharp drop in home loan applications.

"There's a lot of other factors, but interest rates are the primary thing that's shifting. And we, Treasury, the Reserve Bank, all the major banks tell us that house prices will return to growth in the medium term," Ms O'Neil told the ABC last week.

Senate launches housing inquiry

Yesterday, the Senate agreed to establish an inquiry into housing, which will examine the National Housing Accord, recent government policy including an expansion of the 5 per cent deposit scheme and the changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing.

Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg claimed senators had not been given sufficient time to examine these issues, and the six-month inquiry would "finally get to the bottom" of housing concerns.

Andrew Bragg flagged his intention to use a new Senate inquiry to examine the government's tax changes. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Confidence has been shaken since the federal budget up-ended the two-decade old tax treatment on investment properties, which banks and builders say has caused a slowdown in new home loan applications, and seen sharp falls in house prices in some cities.

But recent Bureau of Statistics data shows while there has been an overall slowdown in activity, new investor loans for the construction and purchase of new dwellings are at their highest level on record.

The federal government explicitly allowed new dwellings to remain eligible to be negatively geared to attract more investor capital into new supply, and away from old dwellings.

World.title: Australia's national debt has hit $1 trillion but there's another figure that's more important
World.content:
Shakespeare may well have been onto something when one of his characters in Hamlet uttered these immortal words: "Neither a borrower nor a lender be."

Unfortunately, Polonius's parting advice to his son — that lending to friends can result in the loss of both cash and comrades — seems to have been consigned to the dustbin of history.

For the past 50 years, debt in almost every conceivable category and country has risen to extraordinary levels, to the point where we have largely become desensitised to the trend.

This week, however, as we hit yet another credit milestone, the dirty D-word struck a chord with the broader population.

Australian government gross debt ticked above $1 trillion for the first time in history.

And for a nation that has largely been in lockstep with the United States since the end of World War II, the occasion coincided with American public debt levels soaring to $US40 trillion ($56 trillion).

Given the US dollar is the global reserve currency and therefore determines interest rates for the rest of the world, the events in Washington and the deterioration in America's economic standing are potentially more concerning for us.

Rates to rise

Australia's debt, when compared to the size of the economy, is negligible alongside that of most other developed nations.

At 32 per cent of GDP, we rank well down the debt list.

Germany's debt pile is at a concerning 70 per cent of GDP, the United Kingdom at 95 per cent, the US at 125 per cent and Japan at an astonishing 250 per cent.

"You'd rather be here in Australia in regards to public debt," says independent economist Saul Eslake.

But according to the former Bank of America Merrill Lynch chief economist, we have no cause for complacency.

After borrowing big during the COVID-19 crisis, with short-term loans at ultra-cheap rates, Eslake explains that we now face the prospect of much higher global interest rates and repayments as those loans roll over.

As it is, despite our superior financial position and our Triple-A credit rating, Australia has almost always had to pay a premium when it comes to interest rates. And that will only get worse.

Australian national debt has passed $1 trillion. (ABC News: Michael Janda)

Plenty of debt, shortage of courage

Debt, of itself, is no bad thing.

It's the capacity to repay that is vital. And in recent years, governments across the globe have decided that, rather than impose financial discipline, they'll simply borrow more to finance the repayments.

Here in Australia, debt routinely has become a political football but despite all the goal kicking, little has been done to solve the problem.

In the aftermath of the Global Financial Crisis, Australia notched up a decade of deficits during a resources export boom, before flinging open the chequebook to fund the nation through the pandemic.

"While it was right to go into debt during COVID, we shouldn't be running deficits, as we are doing, when the economy is close to full employment," Eslake argues.

With an electorate demanding more services and spending on health, disability support, child and aged care along with a sharp rise in defence, the money, he says, has to come from somewhere.

"No-one is willing or courageous or honest enough to tell voters that if you want all this extra spending, someone will have to pay for it," he says.

That means, either much higher taxes, or a big cut in spending. But Australians won't accept either.

While we might bask in the satisfaction that, when it comes to government debt, we're not in that much of a pickle, our debt problems lie elsewhere.

Australian household debt is at an eye-watering 190 per cent of household income, mostly due to real estate. (ABC News: John Gunn)

We may be wooden spooners with public debt but with household debt, we're vying for Olympic gold.

Australian household debt is at an eye-watering 190 per cent of household income.

Canada isn't too far behind with 180 per cent, New Zealand at 166 per cent, the UK at 118 per cent and the US at around half our level at 92 per cent of household income.

Mostly attached to real estate, that debt exposure makes Australians more vulnerable to interest rate movements than most other countries.

America's risk profile on the rise

The tectonic plates are shifting.

During the past few weeks, money markets have pushed up interest rates on 30-year US government bonds to the highest level in almost 20 years.

Bonds, essentially, are IOUs that are traded on the open market. They determine the cost of almost everything; home loans, credit cards and stock markets.

Global investors now view America as a higher risk proposition as their trust in America's economic standing is beginning to slip. So, they are demanding higher interest rates on loans.

Loading...

When Donald Trump first came to power in 2016, US debt stood at $US20 trillion. It's now doubled in 10 years. It has risen more than 20 per cent since he resumed power last year.

Tax cuts, huge spending and now a war with seemingly no end.

America's annual interest bill on its debt now totals just shy of $US1 trillion, which is more than the US defence budget and the third biggest budget expense after social security and medicare.

That's why Donald Trump is desperate to lower interest rates.

"I worry that Trump is trashing America's standing and slowly eroding the US dollar and Treasury bonds as a safe haven for investors," Eslake says.

The Congressional Budget Office estimates that within the next eight years, America's debt to GDP ratio will blow out to 137 per cent.

When asked how he sees all this ending, Eslake's reply is succinct.

"Badly," he says.

It means American interest rates will remain higher for longer and, given Australian interest rates historically have been at a premium to the US, higher rates here as well.

"There's nothing Australia can do about it other than to try to repair our own budget situation," he explains.

Rather than address the root cause of the problem, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant has outlined a plan to buy back US government bonds in an effort to muscle down interest rates.

Loading...

And in recent weeks, he helped orchestrate a joint rescue plan for Japan's ailing currency as both countries waded into the market to snap up yen for the first time in decades.

It was yet another move that hinted of cracks within the US financial system.

Cynics couldn't help but join the dots.

Japan is the biggest foreign owner of US government debt and, if it was forced to raise cash alone, it may need to sell US government bonds.

That would push US interest rates higher, something a hugely indebted America can't afford.

World.title: European nations condemn major Israeli settlement plans in West Bank
World.content:
France, Italy, Britain and Germany have jointly condemned a major settlement project in the West Bank and called on Israel to end settlement expansion in the occupied Palestinian territory.

The joint statement by the major European powers came after the Israeli government announced it would open up construction tenders for a residential property project called E1 in the occupied West Bank.

"At a time of grave instability in the West Bank with unprecedented levels of violence by settlers against civilians, and serious restrictions on the Palestinian economy, this decision is even more concerning," the countries said in a joint statement.

They urged Israel "to retract these plans immediately and end its expansion of settlements in the West Bank".

"The decision by the Israeli government to publish bid offers for construction projects within the framework of the E1 settlers' project is unacceptable."

The planned E1 development sits in the occupied West Bank just outside Jerusalem. (ABC News)

Plans to develop the E1 project, a 12-square-kilometre area on the outskirts of Jerusalem, are decades old but never been formally proceeded with.

However, the outbreak of the war between Israel and Hamas revived Israeli ambitions.

The development would kick the local Bedouin community out and replace it with 3,401 homes and a new road.

In January this year the Israeli government announced plans to start construction, and authorities opened bidding to construct more than 1,200 homes in the area this week.

UK Foreign Minister David Miliband said he delivered the joint message directly to his Israeli counterpart Gideon Saar.

Mr Saar then responded publicly on social media site X, saying he rejected "outright" Mr Miliband's statement and "the patronising tone of his words".

"The Jewish people have the right to live throughout the Land of Israel, just as the British have the right to live in London and throughout the United Kingdom," Mr Saar wrote.

At the time, far-right Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich said the development of E1 would "bury" the idea of a Palestinian state.

Aviv Tatarsky, a researcher at Ir Amim, told the ABC in January that the plans would effectively break the West Bank in two.

"It would mean there's no Palestinian contiguity and there's no way to create a viable Palestinian state," he said.

Hundreds of thousands of Israelis have settled among millions of Palestinians in land captured by Israel in a 1967 war.

Nearly all countries and a range of UN bodies consider that such settlements violate international law.

Israel disputes this, citing historical and biblical ties to the land.

ABC/AFP/Reuters

World.title: Loggers avoid environmental laws by labelling operations 'road maintenance'
World.content:
Loggers in New South Wales have felled about 1,000 trees, including habitat for threatened species, but avoided environmental protections by labelling the operations "road maintenance".

The Forestry Corporation of NSW operation in Glenbog State Forest has been called "logging in disguise", with conservationists and legal advocates arguing the corporation took advantage of a "legal loophole" they say could expose 50,000 kilometres of roadside forest to unregulated logging.

Forestry Corporation's road management operation involved taking out 21 truckloads of timber, according to Andrew Wong, an environmental campaigner and executive director of Wilderness Australia.

"This looked like a logging operation, not a road management operation," he said.

The logging took place in Glenbog State Forest in south-east NSW, a location believed to be a stronghold for the critically endangered greater glider.

While trees used as dens by greater gliders typically incur a 50 metre buffer from logging for protection, the operation was conducted under more relaxed laws governing road maintenance, and those protections did not apply.

Logging occurred within 50m of nine greater glider dens (including this one) — an activity that would breach exclusion zones, had it been regulated as commercial logging. (Supplied: Wilderness Australia)

"I think the New South Wales public would be really concerned if they thought that Forestry Corp were able to carry out logging in state forests that didn't comply with the conditions that were intended to provide some level of protection for wildlife," Justine Emerson, a lawyer for the Environmental Defenders Office (EDO), said.

Forestry Corporation did not answer specific questions about the forest operations, but a spokesperson said the operation was contained within the previously disturbed footprint of the road corridor.

"The work in January included some tree removal to enable machinery to access the road and safely carry out works, as well as removal of vegetation that had regrown on the road edge to maintain the road at a suitable width.

"While there is sometimes an opportunity to recover some timber rather than mulching trees within the forest, the purpose of road maintenance works is to improve access and safety for the many community members who use and rely on these roads."

An environmental campaigner, Andrew Wong, estimates at least 1,000 logs over 20cm in diameter were removed and taken to a mill. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Forestry law vs planning law

Earlier this year, Forestry Corporation began an operation in Glenbog State Forest under NSW planning laws, that allows it to maintain roads within NSW state forests.

Documents show the road maintenance was planned across 90 kilometres of road within Glenbog and so far, 2.7km was completed.

Mr Wong estimated at least 1,000 mature trees, some around 100 years old, were removed, resulting in at least 21 truckloads of timber that were then taken to a mill for processing and sale.

Andrew Wong, an environmental campaigner and executive director of Wilderness Australia. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

The environmental assessment completed by Forestry Corporation prior to the operation said the loggers would contain maintenance work to areas that had already been disturbed.

In one section of the operation, clearing occurred up to 10 metres beyond the roadside verges on both sides of the road.

"It was just shocking to see what they'd done. I've seen a lot of roadside management before. This was entirely different," Mr Wong said.

"As far as we know, this is the first time they've ever undertaken what looks like for-profit management."

For this reason, the EDO said the operation was not a road maintenance operation but a logging operation that should have been conducted under NSW forestry laws and regulated by the NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA).

Justine Emerson says in her view, the operation was not road maintenance but logging. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

A spokesperson for the NSW EPA said they were aware of community concerns regarding the road maintenance work in Glenbog.

"The NSW EPA is currently assessing information in relation to this matter. As this assessment is ongoing, it is inappropriate to comment further."

Aboriginal corporation receives restorative justice compensation Traditional owners say a $450,000 fine won't replace the six centuries-old giant trees illegally felled by NSW Forestry Corporation.

James Jooste, CEO of Australian Forestry Products Association, said the idea that the operation was logging in disguise was a "supposition from an activist group who will do anything to desperately try and shut down an industry".

"This is not a Trojan Horse. This is not a loophole. This is practical use of a product or a tree that is felled, that can be milled for a critical product," he said

"We are absolutely comfortable that the maintenance of roads in the forests that yields some trees that can go into mills is a completely practical use of those trees.

"I think that the community would have an expectation that that is the case."

James Jooste believes if trees removed for road maintenance can be milled, they should be. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Threatened species habitat logged

Under forestry laws, Forestry Corporation are required to conduct more thorough surveys for greater gliders than under planning laws.

Forestry Corporation's environmental assessment said threatened species, such as the greater glider were not likely to be impacted by the operation because the work would be conducted within the existing footprint of the road.

However, logging occurred within 50m of nine greater glider dens — an activity that would breach exclusion zones, had it been regulated as commercial logging.

Do you know more? Email angelaheathcote@protonmail.com or contact her on signal: @angeh.36

"What that does, is it removes really important habitat for that species…. They need to be able to walk across canopies, to be able to access food, to be able to access other den trees, because they maintain many different den trees within a home range," WWF ecologist Dr Kita Ashman said.

The potential threats to greater gliders meant the operation might not have been lawful, even if it was road maintenance, Ms Emerson said.

"There's also a question in terms of the Biodiversity Conservation Act that are available for threatened species in New South Wales. It's an offence to harm the habitat of the threatened species," she said.

Mr Wong said if the loophole was not closed, management activities, such as road maintenance, would become profitable and the scale of those activities would increase as a result.

Fight for forestry future The NSW forestry industry is calling for secure access to timber as the proposed Great Koala National Park locks up resources and recent closures of Victorian and Western Australian sectors raise fears for the future of native logging.

"There are 50,000km of roads in New South Wales state forest… The scale of it so great, they could probably do as much logging as they would do within about four or five years of all state forest logging in New South Wales," Mr Wong says.

But the industry said there was no motivation for loggers to do this.

"We have 2 million hectares of state forests that are managed every year under wood supply agreements. We are not in a position where we need to go out on roads that have been maintained and with trees felled, that have to go into those mills to keep a sustainable industry," Mr Jooste said.

World.title: China was making too many cars. They turned to Australia to offload them
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Holden, Ford, Toyota, Nissan, Mitsubishi. For years these are the brands which have dominated the driveways of Australian homes. Now brands such as XPeng, Zeekr, Haval, GAC, Geely, Chery and Leapmotor are competing for customers – and you probably know someone who drives one, even if you don’t yourself … yet. One in every three vehicles sold in Australia in the first six months of this year was made in China. There are at least 10 Chinese automotive companies selling more than 20 individual brands, mostly EVs and plug-in hybrids. And more are coming. Names such as BAW, Changan, Forthing and Nio, all hoping to make a mark in what is widely considered the most competitive car market in the world. But none has yet made the impact of BYD, which launched in Australia with the hopeful moniker Build Your Dreams in 2022, before rebranding its vehicles with the shorter and more palatable initialism soon after. There was scepticism when, not long after launch, its executives told a packed media room that it would be a top-five brand in Australia in 2025, and then continue to grow. For a new brand with only a handful of models, it seemed incredible hubris. But in mid-year 2026, BYD is ahead of schedule. Related Article Good Weekend Ocean views, quiet neighbours and a $165,000 price tag: The other property boom The scale of the appetite for the Chinese auto giant’s cars was evident when the vast BYD Zhengzhou ship sailed into Melbourne in June, with almost 5000 vehicles on board the 200-metre-long floating showroom. BYD had mobilised the shipment in response to the demand for “greener” vehicles in Australia. The same month, the company sold almost 19,000 vehicles here – just 243 sales short of Toyota. The last time a brand beat Toyota in the monthly sales race was in May 2011 – and that was Holden. BYD local chief operating officer Stephen Collins says technology is now a key factor being sought by Australian motorists, who were open to new brands who could deliver.



It hasn’t all been smooth sailing on BYD’s Australian ascent, though. The champagne that was no doubt flowing following the brand’s best-ever month in June would have quickly soured when, in July, it emerged that more than 1200 customers had been sold 2025-build vehicles, not the 2026 models they had paid for. A BYD spokesman was reported as saying it was due to an “administrative error”, and the company has since offered all those affected the option of a full refund. In May, the federal opposition called for a security review into whether any Chinese EVs should remain on the list of taxpayer-funded cars available to parliamentarians, with opposition special minister of state James McGrath describing them as “effectively rolling Chinese data centres”. Legacy brands are watching the newcomers in the Australian market. The local CEO of Korean auto giant Hyundai, Don Romano, bristles when asked if he is surprised at the speed at which BYD had grown here. “I think there’s a big difference between growth at any cost and growth organically,” he said. Vice-president of sales and marketing of Toyota, Australia’s best-selling marque, John Pappas says that something will have to give. “There are all these other brands coming, but the market itself is not growing. So it’s going to be a challenging environment for some of these brands to be sustainable,” he says. BYD might be the headline act, but it is only the tip of a very long spear. Few brands demonstrate the automotive gold rush under way in China better than Dreame, a home electronics company most famous for robotic vacuum cleaners after launching its first stick vacuum in 2018. The brand claims that within the next 18 months, Dreame cars will be for sale in Australia – though details of the SUV range have yet to be revealed – with the brand exploring retail outlets such as Harvey Norman as a substitute for a traditional dealership network. The plan, presumably, is to allow you to buy a couch, a TV and a vacuum cleaner – and then the car you need to get them home. “There are legacy brands who just believe their repeat customers are always going to be there. If we can come in and really showcase the value of our brand, there’s a gap there where we believe customers will transition through,” says Dreame’s Australian manager James Moore. The speed of this change to our new-car market is staggering. In 2020, 30,000 cars sold in Australia were made in China (and in 2019 it was more like 17,000). Over the first six months of 2026, that number was almost 200,000. China is now the single biggest source of origin for vehicles sold in Australia, snapping a 28-year record held by Japan. Helping, too, is that brands like Tesla also source their vehicles from China.



Several events have driven this growth. Over the past five years here, international conflicts have spiked petrol prices, inflation-driven rate rises have hurt household budgets, government incentives have accelerated the adoption of greener vehicles, wait times for certain legacy manufacturers have spiralled, and the 2025 introduction of the ever-tightening New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (which fines brands that don’t meet it) has driven a move to rush EVs to market. Meanwhile, a Chinese manufacturing glut, which has prompted authorities there to clamp down on new car-making facilities and price-cutting wars, inspired company executives to look outwards a few years ago. Europe and the US both have domestic automotive industries to protect. Australia does not, and so has some of the lowest barriers to entry on the planet. Gas meets match. Related Article Good Weekend A scientist was scalped by a machine in her lab. Then her own seaweed research helped mend the wound Mike Costello, an auto analyst at Cox Automotive and Manheim Australia, says that China had over-produced for its local market and started looking for export markets. “China leads the world in all things to do with electrification, and so they recognised that they could really steal a march on everybody as we moved into this new, electrified world,” he says. “They also knew that, through sheer economies of scale or through government help or through really low-cost manufacturing, they could get a leg-up on price as well.” That, says Costello, is a critical point. Chinese vehicles are often cheaper than their rivals, sport more equipment and features on their cheapest, entry-level models and with world-class battery technology. For perspective, the Toyota RAV4 is one of the nation’s bestselling vehicles, and a plug-in hybrid version of this mega-popular SUV arrived in Australia in June. The cheapest version is $58,840 before any on-road costs. The similarly sized Starray from Chinese brand Geely is $37,490. Brand loyalty is suddenly rather expensive. On the surface, the consumer benefits most. The arrival of this army of new brands is driving down prices significantly. But, says Costello, one of the few things not included in the sticker price of a new brand’s vehicle is the implied security of legacy. “The one thing the Chinese brands don’t have is long-term proven residual values and long-term proven reliability in Australia. And that’s not to say that they won’t have those things. But if you buy a Toyota or a Honda or a Hyundai, you know, to a degree, that this vehicle is going to do the job,” he says.



“My two cents is that these vehicles are built to the same standards as pretty much anything else in terms of how sophisticated they are. But only time will unlock the truth or the falsity of that. The question we have is that, in a position where we are going to have 70 or 80 different brands from all over the world in this market, including 30-odd from China, can a market of our size truly support that in a sustainable, profitable, long-term way? ‘Are all these brands going to survive? I think the general consensus is no.’ “The general sentiment in the industry is that it’s extremely difficult to imagine that we won’t see some brands pack up and leave because they just can’t sell enough vehicles to justify staying. Now, that may include some traditional brands, but it will also include some of these Chinese brands.” It’s a thought echoed by Hyundai’s Romano, who suggests the collapse of brands in Australia – newcomer or legacy – could have a devastating ripple effect on customers and the market more broadly. “The question is, are all of these brands going to survive? And I think the general consensus from every manufacturer is no. So the question then becomes, when they leave, who holds the warranty liability? I think it’s a worry that some of the big dealer groups are holding onto a number of brands that may or may not be around – and I’m not talking about Chinese brands, it could be any brand.” Related Article Good Weekend Ant was at the peak of his career. Then it clicked: he had to put himself on the line The dominoes are wobbling. TrueEV, the Australian company responsible for selling and servicing models from the Chinese brand XPeng, had administrators appointed in March before closing its only Sydney showroom. XPeng’s Chinese HQ has since stepped in to establish operations in Australia and will set up its own dealer network for sales and servicing, in the same way brands like Toyota, Nissan or Mitsubishi are operated here. In July, the distributor for the French brand Peugeot relinquished its distribution rights for the brand, with the French marque’s future here currently uncertain, though it insists it will continue in some capacity.

World.title: Exclusive Brethren secretly paid far-right activists to perform stunts disrupting the federal election
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Elders of a wealthy Christian sect secretly paid bundles of cash to far-right activists for an “influence campaign” to disrupt Albanese government appearances during the last federal election. An investigation by this masthead has uncovered a digital trail of evidence revealing how the church, formerly known as the Exclusive Brethren, mobilised far-right figures around the country to track and heckle candidates from Labor and the Greens, along with independents, as part of a wider multimillion-dollar campaign for then-Liberal leader Peter Dutton. When far-right influencer Laurence McIntyre yelled at Prime Minister Anthony Albanese about immigration on the first day of the election campaign, it looked like just a random attack from the fringes of politics. But it was one of almost a dozen far-right stunts this masthead has traced back to the Brethren’s dirty tricks campaign. That includes – six political and church sources say – when the prime minister was twice ambushed in his hotel lobby by far-right figures boasting of being fed “private intel” on his location. The church categorically denies any involvement. Leaked communications, insider accounts and social media footage now reveal the extent of the Brethren’s role in the 2025 election, as a spokesman for the sect, the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church, prepares to give evidence on Friday to a parliamentary inquiry examining the scandal. Four sources independently referred to a “duffel bag of cash” provided by senior Brethren members to a key right-wing figure who flew around the country helping coordinate the “influence campaign”.



The motley crew of agitators enlisted for stunts include McIntyre, who has links to neo-Nazis, as well as fringe politicians and pro-Putin conspiracists. The idea, according to five people with knowledge of the operation, was to disrupt the campaigns of Coalition opponents and push an anti-immigration message using already-notorious figures from outside the church. This would mask the Brethren’s involvement from the public – and from their own flock. Far-right figure Laurence McIntyre (in cap), heckles Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen Senior Brethren elders used flight tracking apps to follow Albanese’s plane as it moved from city to city during the campaign, according to four sources who spoke anonymously due to safety concerns. At times, Brethren gophers lay in wait with far-right influencers to follow the prime minister’s car to hotels and events and even joined in the heckling of politicians. This masthead has sighted internal communications confirming senior Brethren elders were involved in coordinating the stunts, including paying influencers. Thousands of dollars for the headline-grabbing antics changed hands. This masthead has seen evidence of payments behind many of the stunts and sources verify the rest, but has chosen not to name the church figures involved to protect those sources. Some described cash being handed over in car parks and at “discreet meets” with Brethren or through intermediaries. The stunts were filmed and splashed across right-wing media and social channels. Some were also posted by conservative lobby group Advance, which itself received $655,000 in political donations from Brethren businessmen last year. But Advance denied knowing who was involved or playing any role in Brethren campaigning. Loading



The Brethren church has itself consistently denied any involvement in the election, conceding that only its individual parishioners campaigned, not the church itself. Asked about the right-wing agitators, a spokesman said: “If members did donate or have involvement with [any political party or third-party groups], that was under their name not the church’s.” He added that the church “completely rejects antisemitism”. Key Brethren figures identified in the evidence and approached individually by this masthead denied they had planned, organised or funded the stunts. When asked about tracking Albanese’s plane, one elder said: “Anyone with a flight tracking app can do that.” Two of the MPs on the committee now examining the Brethren’s conduct at the last election – Labor’s Jerome Laxale and independent Monique Ryan – were themselves targeted in the stunts. Following the Coalition’s crushing election loss, sources within the church say elders and ordinary members have begun shifting their allegiance to Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. They warn that “the Brethren’s well-oiled influence machine” is not finished in politics yet, as an image surfaces showing a member campaigning for One Nation in Victoria last year. A member of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church campaigning for One Nation in rural Victoria at the 2025 federal election. Some within the sect say world leader, “Man of God” Bruce Hales, has signalled approval of One Nation’s policies, though that message has not appeared in his printed ministry. There is no evidence Hales was directly involved in organising or paying for the stunts.



Three church and political sources say senior Brethren members have trained in campaigning with Donald Trump’s MAGA movement in the United States. A Brethren business in Iowa hosted an election event in May featuring US Vice President JD Vance. Concerned Christian businessmen In early 2025, well before the May election, a few well-placed figures in the hard-right heard of a discreet opportunity. A group of “concerned Christian businessmen” were eager to stir things up on the campaign trail, to set the conditions for a Coalition victory – and they were willing to pay cash. The Brethren seeking help from some of the “spicier” elements of the right all held influential positions within the church’s hierarchy. The sources say they were referred to as “the client” and often acted through the Brethren company Sante Global. Between March and the May election day, about a dozen Brethren elders coordinated with far-right figures across the country, mostly using encrypted messaging apps, to pull off stunts targeting Albanese and Labor, as well as “teal” candidates and the Greens in Queensland, NSW and Victoria. At times, a small number of people connected to the Coalition were aware of the Brethren stunts, but sources say staffers didn’t appear to understand the full picture, and the party hierarchy was not involved. As the effort was ramped up, this masthead has confirmed that a booking was made in the name of Sante Group at a Sydney golf club on April 1, 2025, bringing together state leaders from the Brethren, with a small clutch of their far-right helpers.



In the Brethren’s wider multimillion-dollar election effort for the Coalition, its members turned out to campaign undercover at polling booths in blue Liberal t-shirts despite their usual edict to shun the outside world. But now elders wanted to talk about more creative political strategies. Among the far-right figures invited was vlogger Chris De Bruyne, who goes by Chriscoveries online. De Bruyne’s wife, Edwina Bull, endorsed posters during the campaign which were linked to the Brethren. These included the mysterious “Make Australia happy again” signs spotted on roadsides that April, reflecting a Brethren call to arms. For weeks, De Bruyne had already been sharing and distributing many of the stunts in the Brethren operation. Some were carried out by his associates, one a pro-Putin agitator, and another: former Liberal Barclay McGain, who was fired from an MP’s office for posting racist comments in 2019 and now heads CPAC Australia. Anti-lockdown “freedom party” founder Morgan C Jonas also shared and took part in some of the stunts. Posters he endorsed during the campaign were displayed by Brethren members – and flagged as non-compliant by the Australian Electoral Commission, which confirmed it is investigating wider concerns about Brethren involvement in 2025. A Brethren member in shorts and a Liberal Party t-shirt puts up a poster endorsed by Morgan C Jonas. Jonas, who like De Bruyne has been linked to Advance campaigns, refused to answer questions, including about whether he was paid for taking part in the Brethren operation or endorsing their signage. De Bruyne didn’t respond to requests for comment. The stunts are still prominently displayed on the website of the political lobbying firm he runs, Australian Firebrand, as an example of its recent “campaigns”.

World.title: A new suburb will be unlocked in Melbourne’s west. For Sarah, it’s too late
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaGo west A new suburb will be unlocked in Melbourne’s west. For Sarah, it’s too late Cassandra Morgan August 21, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A new suburb with 12,000 homes and seven schools has been approved in a bid to keep pace with the population boom in Melbourne’s west – the fastest-growing region in Australia. The Carroll government has given the green light to a structure plan for Melton East, in a signal to developers to seek permits to start building in the new suburb while authorities deliver the required infrastructure, including the new schools and open space covering the equivalent of five MCGs. There are also plans for four community hubs, three new arterial roads and five bridges, as well as cycling and pedestrian connections, while the new Melton Hospital is already under construction in nearby Cobblebank. Melton East is expected to be home to more than 36,000 people while supporting about 1600 jobs once it is fully developed by the middle of the century.



By 2050, the overall population in Melbourne’s west is expected to double to 1.8 million people, and an alliance of major local employers, councils and community leaders argues the region needs a formal housing strategy to co-ordinate and deliver plans across the different local government areas. Related Article Go west This western suburb could be our second CBD, but residents fear the dream is under threat In the next decade, 10,000 homes need to be built in Melbourne’s west annually to cope with demand, predominantly in Melton and Wyndham. That is roughly in line with the state government’s plans, but in some areas, particularly the outer-west, new builds aren’t keeping up with population growth, says the West of Melbourne Economic Development Alliance (WoMEDA). That is especially true for affordable homes close to the region’s biggest employers, such as hospitals. The push for a sweeping housing strategy is one in a suite of demands WoMEDA has for all political parties ahead of the November state election, one year on from the alliance’s West of Melbourne Summit, presented with The Age.



“As the fastest growing region in Australia, the west of Melbourne needs an integrated approach,” said WoMEDA chair Peter Dawkins. Melbourne could follow the NSW government’s approach of a decade ago, establishing a western city commission (modelled off the now defunct Greater Sydney Commission) to create a whole-of-west plan, the alliance says. Sydney’s commission created an ambitious 40-year blueprint to transform the city into a three-CBD metropolis – Parramatta being one. The goal is similar for Melbourne’s Sunshine, with the Labor government prioritising the suburb for major infrastructure, including the airport rail link. But there is no equivalent body driving change across the whole of the city’s west, according to WoMEDA executive director Giulia Baggio. “It would need to be as non-partisan as possible and involve the three levels of government, private sector and community, overseen by a state government agency,” Baggio said.



“It could develop, say a 20- or 30-year plan. “Rather than allow housing to keep sprawling, especially across our greenfield communities, a West of Melbourne Commission could oversee a curated, intelligent design backed up by a staged, funded plan on a development timeline.” For some residents of Melbourne’s west, it is already too late. On Hope Way in Tarneit, Sarah McDougall is packing up. Sarah McDougall is moving from Melbourne’s west because she says it is too busy and infrastructure is not keeping pace with population growth. Simon Schluter Boxes are strewn through her two-bedroom brick duplex, which she bought in 2013 when these suburbs were quieter and sparser. Her dog paces restlessly in her small fenced backyard, and too-dim street lights glow above cars sprawled on grass and driveways beside the narrow street.



“It used to be, get out of Hoppers and open countryside to Melton,” said McDougall, who is in her early 40s. “Now, it’s almost to the point of suffocating because it’s all filled in and there’s no space any more. “End of the year, I’m gone.” McDougall is retreating to Ballarat for its open space, in a backfiring of the boom for the city’s west as it is choked with industry, warehouses and bottle-necked traffic. While new housing is built, infrastructure isn’t keeping pace, McDougall says, a concern shared by WoMEDA. About half of the workforce in Melbourne’s west has to leave the region to reach their workplace.



Under the state government, a suite of new tertiary institutions are in train, including a Melton TAFE and a tech school in Brimbank. In the immediate term, though, TAFE places at Victoria University and The Gordon in Werribee need to double to meet demand, the alliance argues. Melton Mayor Lara Carli adds that while a new TAFE is expected to open in Cobblebank in 2028, “our city has no university”. Former premier Jacinta Allan at the site of the new Melton Hospital in Cobblebank last year. Wayne Taylor “Housing needs to be matched by investment in transport, roads, education, services and employment precincts,” she said. WoMEDA is also asking for expedited electrification of the Melton line – it was promised in 2018 – and planning for the Suburban Rail Loop’s western end, as annual average population growth of 3 per cent puts “enormous strain” on transport in Melbourne’s west.



The state government is working to finalise the project design for Melton electrification, with the new local station due to open on September 1. On Friday, it will also open consultation for a structure plan to unlock another new suburb called Merrifield North, a 970-hectare precinct that is expected to support 4700 jobs across industries including warehousing, transport and logistics. “The plans for Melton East and Merrifield North are about building connected places for more Victorians to live, work and thrive,” Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny said. Victoria continued to build more housing than any other state, a government spokesman added, while acknowledging that “we know there is more to do”. But opposition planning spokesman David Southwick says that because of “Labor’s neglect, housing and basic infrastructure hasn’t kept up with the growth” in Melbourne’s fastest growing suburbs.



Related Series

Go west Go west “Under a Liberal and Nationals government, we will work with the community to deliver housing and the infrastructure into Melbourne’s fastest growing suburbs where we know people want to live,” Southwick said. The Victorian Greens, meanwhile, have committed to doubling public housing across the state, “because essential workers increasingly can’t even find somewhere to rent, let alone somewhere they can afford”, Footscray candidate Elena Pereyra said. The Greens have also promised $245 million to improve the frequency of regional trains and coaches, and $270 million to reform Melbourne’s bus network, starting in the city’s west. McDougall won’t stick around to wait for those changes.



When she makes the move to Ballarat, it’ll take her about an hour on the train to travel to her workplace in Sunshine. That’s an hour she’d otherwise spend in peak-hour traffic, driving to and from Tarneit every day. Standing in the dark outside her home on Hope Way, she says freedom is one of the things she’s most looking forward to.
